Our proposed method, called "Re-Initialisation", involves resetting the weights of a pre-trained model to their original state before processing each new task, using only the initial data and then stopping the training process. Counter to the typical outcome of fine-tuning, Re-Initialisation exhibits a capacity for learning new tasks without suffering significant loss of performance on previous tasks. A thorough investigation of our method's behavior suggests that its success stems from its ability to avoid information overlap between successive tasks, thus preventing the typical phenomenon of "catastrophic forgetting".

As social media continues to grow in popularity, it has become a preferred platform for people to express their opinions, yet it also poses significant threats due to the spread of toxic and violent content. This problem has prompted researchers to develop methods for identifying hate speech, a key challenge in maintaining a safe and responsible online environment. We have focused on this issue by proposing an innovative, two-part framework for hate speech detection. The first component combines text and user information to identify relevant features, while the second uses these selected features, extracted from text and user data, to classify posts as hate speech. Through our evaluation of the proposed framework on multiple datasets, we have achieved better accuracy and F1 scores compared to existing solutions.

We investigate the behavior of large networks of Type-I neurons, where each node is modeled using the Hodgkin-Huxley conductance formalism and connected in a mean-field manner. The degree distribution of these networks determines their behavior as they approach a critical threshold, whether they transition into a state of synchronized oscillation or remain in a state of stochastic irregularity. The present study builds upon previous work by considering various degree distributions, expanding upon earlier research which focused solely on networks with an exponential degree distribution. The ability to analyze and compare degree distributions enables a deeper understanding of how network architecture affects the transition into oscillatory behavior. The findings from this study are further validated through numerical simulations.

Recent years have seen increasing interest in Automatic Program Repair (APR) with
numerous approaches being developed to address this challenging task. Most APR
methods proposed so far aim to find a repair by representing the semantics of
programs using mathematical logic and searching for an interpretation that meets
certain repair criteria. However, these methods face significant limitations in
covering the vast search space of program semantics. In contrast, this paper
explores the potential of adversarial patch generation, a technique initially used
for manipulating visual representations, to address APR. Our proposed method
involves generating patches using a GAN model that pits a generator producing
patches against a discriminator that differentiates authentic and fake patches.
Our evaluation suggests that this approach can efficiently identify potential
repair patches for issues that APR methods struggle with.

This paper introduces a general framework for the capacity region of a single-hop network with multiple transmitters and one receiver using generalized interference as intended causality (GIFC) under specific conditions. By focusing on GIFC with multiple, independent, power-constrained transmitters, we model the channel as a sequence of finite-block-length sequences, treating the transmitters as separate sources of information for the receiver. We establish a fundamental relationship between GIFC capacity and information-spectrum rates, allowing us to achieve GIFC capacity at various block-lengths. We further demonstrate that the resulting capacity region encompasses all rates that satisfy a specific information-spectrum rate pair for any given block-length. This property enables us to show that previously established capacity regions of GIFC with multiple, independent, power-constrained transmitters, using specific criteria (such as successive interference cancellation and maximum transmit power), are subsets of the resulting capacity region for any given block-length. We also establish that these previously established capacity regions are themselves subsets of the resulting capacity region for all possible block-lengths.

This work introduces a novel method for analyzing final state particles emitted in non-central heavy-ion collisions, centered on a novel flow metric. Our research demonstrates that this metric is highly dependent on the collision angle, consistent with expectations, and serves as an effective tool for studying the collision geometry. Furthermore, we investigate how this metric's dependence on the Equation-of-State can be assessed. Our study reveals that this class of flow metrics offers valuable insights into the collision dynamics and can be used to gather information about the properties of the system's state function.

The rapid spread of the COVID-19 pandemic has led to an overwhelming number of cases worldwide, necessitating the development of reliable systems to detect the disease at an early stage. Researchers have turned to machine learning models, particularly deep learning, to analyze patient data and identify potential cases. Despite significant progress, deep learning models often rely on sensitive patient information such as personal data, medical history, and lab results, which must be protected to maintain patient confidentiality. This paper proposes an innovative approach to safeguard patient data by employing adversarial training techniques to develop robust models that can function effectively even with partially missing data. Our method involves training a generator network to introduce random errors in patient data, which is then used to adapt the deep learning model and make it resistant to such distortions. By doing so, the deep learning model can operate accurately even with partially erroneous data. Our study demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach by comparing the performance of our method with other adversarial training methods, revealing that it outperforms them in terms of overall performance. Additionally, we found that our method enhances the model's ability to operate with partially anonymized patient data, thereby protecting sensitive information while maintaining model performance.

Wireless communication systems' reliability is crucial for everyday life, such as remote healthcare and autonomous driving, which necessitate the development of intelligent communication systems. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have the potential to process complex wireless data, like network graphs and channel information. However, traditional GNN models often rely on centralized processing, which can become impractical for large-scale wireless systems due to high communication delays and bandwidth requirements. This could further compromise the real-time processing needed for wireless applications. This study addresses these limitations by introducing a novel decentralized GNN model that leverages edge computing to minimize communication overhead. The proposed model demonstrates superior performance in various wireless systems, such as wireless networks and IoT devices, by effectively predicting wireless metrics like throughput and energy efficiency. The results show that our model outperforms traditional benchmark methods, such as machine learning-based alternatives.

Homicide rates in Brazil are notably higher than those in most other countries, with significant variations observed within the country's territorial boundaries. This research aims to analyze and understand the spatio-temporal patterns of homicides in the state of Goias, by comparing and grouping municipalities based on their homicide rates over an 13-year period from 2002 to 2014. A total of 211 data points consisted of annual homicide rates for each municipality, resulting in 1,653 observations. Using an unsupervised learning approach, this research employed the k-means clustering technique, which identified four distinct groups of municipalities, each characterized by varying levels of homicide incidence. A time-series analysis of each group showed contrasting trends, with three groups experiencing increasing homicide rates over time, while the remaining group exhibited decreasing or relatively stable rates. This study's findings are consistent with existing research on the factors contributing to high homicide rates in Brazil, including demographic characteristics, socioeconomic conditions, and regional influences.

We propose a new adaptive learning rate method for stochastic gradient descent that mirrors the SGLD algorithm. Unlike the conventional approach, this technique doesn't rely on a fixed covariance matrix, instead utilizing a dynamically adjusted matrix that reflects the unique characteristics of each iteration. Our method is rooted in a quadrature-based approach and is capable of being applied to a range of optimization problems beyond stochastic gradient descent. We provide empirical evidence demonstrating that our algorithm outperforms standard SGD by accelerating convergence, while a minor modification also enables it to rival or surpass the accelerated performance of ADAM.

Axions emerge as a prospective explanation for dynamic solar coronal features and the missing mass in the universe.  Various studies have examined the Sun's potential as a target for axion research.  A key aspect of astrophysical axion research involves determining the likelihood of axion emission and the duration for which this emission occurs.  A proposed experiment, BabyIAXO, aims to utilize the Sun as a target for real-time observations of inverse-Compton scattering of solar thermal x-rays by 3He nuclei.  A comprehensive analysis of the Sun's core has been conducted to establish the expected rate of axion emission per target nucleus.  This study's findings provide a benchmark rate of $1.15 \times 10^{-3}$ axions per nucleus per day.  This rate serves as a reference point for future research and represents an essential step towards the development of BabyIAXO.

The occupation number over time is examined for a bosonic oscillator coupled to heat baths with ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, and uniform spin interactions. By doing this, we can look at how non-equilibrium states in the system change over time, representing a type of dynamical system that has a steady pattern of change. These investigations confirm that a long-term, recurring change in the occupation number occurs, characterizing a type of self-oscillating behavior. The frequency and amplitude of these oscillations are determined by the parameters of the ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic interactions, as well as the characteristics of the heat baths. Additionally, we found that antiferromagnetic interactions in the bosonic oscillator are equivalent to ferromagnetic interactions but with opposite characteristics.

Developing robots that can effectively interact with diverse objects remains a significant challenge in robotics research. Grasping, a crucial aspect of robotic manipulation, requires a thorough understanding of the relationship between a robot's end-effector shape and the object's geometric characteristics. However, existing robotic platforms are often limited by their specific designs, making it difficult to apply previously developed grasping strategies to new robots. To overcome this issue, researchers must employ computational methods that simulate robotic platforms and evaluate different grasping techniques. A crucial step in this process involves creating a comprehensive dataset of simulated grasping information, which can be used to train deep learning models. Our research presents DexGraspNet, a vast dataset of simulated grasping information for diverse objects, tailored to the specifications of the Franka Emika Panda robot. By leveraging the power of computational simulation, our dataset encompasses a wide range of objects, from everyday items to complex industrial products. To generate the dataset, we employed a novel algorithm that incorporates object symmetry to reduce computational costs. The resulting dataset includes over 4 million successful grasps, spanning more than 2,500 objects. To assess the effectiveness of the dataset, we employed a deep learning model that utilizes a graph convolutional neural network to predict grasping information. Our results demonstrate that the deep learning model achieves an impressive 0.988 AUC on the training dataset and 0.934 AUC on the testing dataset. A novel free-breathing T2-weighted MRI sequence, utilizing multi-channel data reconstruction and model-based respiratory compensation, is developed to provide high-quality images in patients with gastroesophageal disease. The approach involves employing a turbo spin-echo sequence to achieve 3D T2-weighted contrast. The sequence is optimized for rapid acquisition time by employing a minimum of 30 phases and utilizing a low number of excitation pulses. To acquire high-quality images in the presence of variable patient respiration, a novel reconstruction approach is designed to provide motion compensation. The method involves dividing the data into segments and using a low-rank matrix completion technique to correct for differences in phase and signal. The resulting images are then refined through an iterative process of non-local means reconstruction. The method is validated through a study of its performance using a large dataset of 50 patients, which compared its image quality to traditional breath-hold T2-weighted images.

Recent advancements in model compression through knowledge distillation have yielded impressive results, allowing larger models to be replaced with more compact ones. However, the majority of these compressions are performed in a supervised manner, with little consideration given to how the model's internal data flows are organized. In this paper, we propose InDistill, a novel approach to unsupervised knowledge distillation that takes into account the model's internal data flows. We achieve this by representing the model's data flows as directed graphs and developing a method to generate training data that accurately captures these flows. Our results demonstrate that InDistill can effectively learn these data flows and significantly improve the model's performance when compared to traditional knowledge distillation methods.

Two submersion functions from the set of two-dimensional real numbers to the set of real numbers are defined, and their level sets are considered as a partition of the plane. These functions can be viewed as a particular type of structure on the plane, referred to as foliations. Our goal is to investigate the relationship between the topological equivalence of these functions and the topological equivalence of the associated foliations. Specifically, we aim to prove that the topological equivalence of linear-like submersion functions implies the topological equivalence of their foliations, and that this implication is also true under certain conditions.

Ecosystems that thrive in arid regions are particularly susceptible to environmental changes due to their limited resource reserves and the significant impact of individual actions. The dynamics of these ecosystems can be influenced by the migration patterns of herbivores, which in turn are guided by vegetation growth. A model that takes into account the connection between the movement of grazing animals and the distribution of vegetation it moves through over dry land is explored through mathematical analysis. The model's solutions are examined through numerical simulations, which reveal complex patterns of coexistence and competition among different plant species. The model's behavior is further evaluated through the analysis of stable states and system boundaries.

A popular dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, we discovered that CountSketch can be compromised when dealing with tailored or adaptively designed inputs. Our research presents a new set of measurements based on the Füredi-Hajnal-Pósa-Lovász shadow removal technique, specifically engineered to counter the adaptability of CountSketch. We found that these modified measurements can be used in CountSketch, resulting in a version that can reliably identify the top elements of a given vector even when presented with adaptively designed inputs.

A Python-based program, ipie, has been developed to run auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo simulations on CPUs and GPUs, offering a flexible and efficient approach with easy-to-use functions and a flexible data structure. The program's performance is demonstrated using a variety of molecular and periodic systems, including the valence bond model, alanine dipeptide dimers, and silicon bulk. Our results show ipie's performance in comparison to Pie, particularly in terms of efficiency with GPU acceleration and efficiency in terms of computational time with CPU and GPU processing. The program's source code is available for public use, and this study provides a comprehensive guide for using ipie, including examples of its application.

High-frequency trading could greatly benefit from quantum computing due to its potential to execute millions of transactions per second.  However, current cloud infrastructure is still reliant on classical technology.  To address this, Quantum Cloud Inc. is developing private networks that allow users to access quantum computing capabilities.  A recent demonstration of this network involved a QCD game on the Quantum Cloud, showcasing the network's ability to run quantum applications in tandem with classical systems.  A QCD game, played out on the network, highlighted the risks of race conditions that could arise in quantum-sensative environments like the Quantum Cloud, leading to unexpected outcomes.  A proposed solution to mitigate these issues involves the use of atomic operations, and it is suggested that this approach could also apply to existing high-frequency trading systems to prevent losses due to race conditions.

This study investigates how sellers and buyers can maximize their overall revenue in a market where intermediaries are present, and auctions are sealed. Initially, we consider a market with a single seller and multiple units of a good. We develop strategies for the seller and buyers to maximize revenue when intermediaries can specify prices for individual units or in bulk. Our analysis reveals that optimal revenue is achieved when the seller prices according to quantity or, in some cases, quantity with a minimum purchase, while the buyers purchase at the minimum price per unit. We extend this research to a market with multiple sellers and find that optimal revenue is achieved when the market is fragmented into sub-markets, each controlled by a single seller, and buyers purchase from the sub-market with the lowest price per unit.

To facilitate abstractive summarization, we've developed an approach that involves generating summaries through entity-level annotations, derived from pre-trained language models, which are then used to outline the key entities and events in a story. This entity-based framework allows for the incorporation of various semantic structures when generating summaries. Our two-phase method begins by extracting essential entities and their roles from the source text, followed by a summary generation process, where the extracted entities are embedded in the context to produce high-quality summaries. Our approach has been tested on the GOSSIP dataset and has demonstrated superior performance in entity-based summary generation, achieving results of 44.47 ROUGE-1 and 23.63 ROUGE-L, which significantly surpass the current state-of-the-art methods.

This research presents new sufficient conditions for differentiating a function with n real variables, where each condition is based on the differentiability of a related function with n-1 variables and satisfies certain relationships on an (n-1)-dimensional hypersurface in R^n.

Human vocal synchronization in social interactions provides valuable information about a person's emotional state, intentions, and levels of engagement. Analyzing this phenomenon, or entrainment, can help researchers and practitioners better understand complex social behaviors. To facilitate easier assessment of entrainment in everyday conversations, we've developed a novel, context-sensitive approach that measures temporal correlations in speech patterns across various time intervals. Our method is particularly adaptable to real-world dialogue data and outperforms alternative metrics in multiple scenarios. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we used this approach to investigate how people talk during a therapy session and identified specific patterns of synchronization associated with certain therapeutic concepts.

A recent study by R\"oder and Panangaden introduced the Lambda category, representing a fundamental component of control theory applied to quantum mechanics, and identified two potential versions, denoted Lambda1 and Lambda2. Focusing on Lambda1, this research paper establish a comprehensive model for its equivalent commutative and symmetric monoidal categories, establish a connection between Lambda1 morphism categories and the category of linear quantum operations, and provide an in-depth analysis of the functors linking Lambda1 to its corresponding QO category, ultimately revealing that every quantum process defined within Lambda1 can be realized through a specific unitary evolution.

Analytical calculations have been performed for two types of quasiparticle excitation energies per particle in systems of up to seven electrons within the fractional quantum Hall effect, for the ground states described by the wave functions derived from the composite fermion theory and Ginzburg-Landau-Chern-Simons-fermion composite excitions. These calculations employed the exact two-body wave functions derived by Fendley. The obtained analytical results are in excellent agreement with the exact energies found in the numerical calculations based on the density-matrix renormalization group method, for the ground states described by the ground states of the composite fermion wave function and the Ginzburg-Landau-Chern-Simons-fermion composite excitions.

In the context of glaciology, particularly when modelling contact problems related to grounding line issues in marine ice sheets, Stokes variational inequalities come into play. This study focuses on a marine ice model with a semi-coercive characteristics, and we explore the convergence of the Galerkin approximation in the finite element method. Although our approach can be broadly applied to other semi-coercive contact problems, our primary interest lies in understanding the behavior of the approximation near the contact area in glaciology.

Galaxy growth is controlled by a balance between the formation of new stars and the loss of mass through galactic outflows. The relationship between these processes is crucial in understanding how galaxies regulate their own growth. Using observations from the VLA and ALMA, we have studied a distant galaxy in a state of rapid star formation. Our analysis reveals a direct connection between the formation of new stars and the speed of galactic outflows. We have observed outflows emerging from regions of intense star formation and escaping through the galaxy's edges. The shape and speed of these outflows change with distance, resulting in slower speeds at greater distances. Our findings suggest that galactic outflows are a result of the pressure from newly formed stars pushing against the galaxy's gas. The galaxy's curved shape allows outflows to escape more easily, and the loss of gas through these outflows may eventually slow the rate of star formation.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we found an inverse correlation between anisotropic initial geometry and anisotropic flow. Additionally, we found that the partonic stage significantly impacted the triangular flow. In collisions involving Au+Au, the partonic stage accounted for approximately 40% of final triangular flow, while in Cu+Cu collisions, this value was around 20%.

This paper introduces the SRF (Synchronous Robotic Framework), a Java-based library designed for controlling robots in a synchronous manner. The SRF allows robots to be controlled in a simultaneous and coordinated fashion, taking into account their actual mechanical limitations. The framework incorporates the following key components: a novel Task API for managing robot operations in a safe and efficient manner, a controller with a preemtive scheduling algorithm, and a device abstraction for encapsulating robot hardware as virtual components. The SRF's technical foundations and its potential for successful application in robot competitions are demonstrated through its use in controlling a robot that won first prize in the 2018 Chinese Open Robotics Competition.

Recent advancements in deep learning have led to impressive performance in autonomous driving tasks such as semantic segmentation. Many studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of transfer learning in achieving state-of-the-art results, with self-supervised learning emerging as a promising alternative. Our research investigates the potential of monocular depth estimation as a pre-training method for semantic segmentation, contrasting it to traditional classification methods. Through comprehensive experiments on the KITTI and Cityscapes datasets, we assess the impact of different pre-training approaches, loss functions, and architecture designs on semantic segmentation. Our findings reveal that depth-based pre-training outperforms classification-based pre-training, with significant benefits in terms of semantic segmentation accuracy. Moreover, we contribute a novel architecture design for depth-based pre-training, comprising a lightweight feature extractor and a depth estimation head, which serves as a suitable starting point for this task.

Let's consider the set of all analytic functions defined within the unit disk in the complex plane, and also the set of all mappings from this disk to itself that preserve the disk's orientation, denoted by $\mathcal{S}$. A specific subclass of $\mathcal{M}$, defined as the set of all mappings from the disk to itself that satisfy certain real-valued conditions, is the focus of our investigation. A particular type of harmonic mapping, known as log-harmonic, is also studied in the context of the class $\mathcal{M}$. By examining relationships between certain real-valued conditions and properties of subharmonic functions, we are able to determine the radius of the disk that remains fixed under a specific type of transformation, defined as the Bohr radius, for a particular subclass of $\mathcal{M}$.

A nonparametric measure of correlation known as Kendall's tau is examined, along with an efficient method for estimating its value from data. The proposed method significantly reduces computational time by analyzing only relevant data points in each calculation, resulting in a time complexity of order O(n) and a relative error rate of  u, where n represents the total number of data pairs. The method of partition has been adapted to achieve this, and the method's accuracy and performance are further validated through series expansions and Monte Carlo tests, which show the method's actual running time and relative error rates conforming to the predicted values of O(n) and  u, respectively. The method's practical usability is demonstrated through a real-world example using data from the London School of Economics' Tau Calculator website.

The integration of Edge Intelligence in the automotive sector has the potential to create intelligent, connected, and safe driving systems, despite the significant privacy risks associated with sharing vehicle data with the cloud. To address these privacy concerns, researchers have developed various mechanisms to safeguard users' data. However, existing solutions often compromise on privacy, edge resource utilization, or accuracy. To overcome these limitations, we propose a framework that utilizes Federated Learning and Differential Privacy to create a decentralized, privacy-preserving Edge Intelligence network. The goal is to develop robust machine learning models capable of detecting potential hazards, such as lane change and collision risks, while maintaining the confidentiality of vehicle sensor data.

This study introduces the concept of Euler characteristic surfaces as a specialized type of category-graded hyper surfaces. We derive the fundamental definitions, discuss their crucial properties and demonstrate their applicability to solve two key problems. Firstly, we address the issue of division by zero in the case of surfaces. Our investigation reveals that these surfaces can be divided into three distinct categories based on their topological characteristics: manifolds with boundaries, surfaces with vanishing boundaries, and Euler characteristic surfaces. Our research specifically focuses on the latter, which cannot be classified as either a manifold with boundary or a signed hypersurface. Secondly, we investigate the possibility of generalizing the Euler characteristic in the context of hyper surface division. Our findings indicate that this characteristic can be extended to the level of surfaces, which is consistent with the established understanding of Euler characteristics for compact surfaces.

Our analysis focuses on an adjusted predator-prey model, incorporating a strong Allee effect and specifically the Holling-Tanner model. In this modified version, both predator and prey populations experience consequences due to low population counts, resulting in the Holling-Tanner model's typical critical curve no longer being a threshold beyond which one or more populations become extinct. Instead, population trends vary depending on initial population values. We have found and proven the existence of unique, coexisting solutions, as well as periodic orbits. Additionally, we have established criteria for the long-term persistence and extinction of both predator and prey populations. These conclusions are supported by numerical simulations.

In a polynomial ring with a single variable, Heidari and Rangipour developed a graded version of the Bak's Lie algebra, which was later used to define the NK_1 algebra over specific types of rings. Building on this concept, a graded variant of the NK_1 algebra is being explored in relation to graded Lie algebras over commutative graded rings with a positive degree one identity. A cohomology theory is also introduced for these NK_1 algebras and their associated cohomology is calculated for particular instances.

This paper examines the influence of off-shell contributions on top quark mass (m_t) determination through a detailed theoretical and phenomenological analysis. A study using parton-level calculations reveals that accounting for off-shell corrections in processes like t-channel production enhances the accuracy of m_t extraction at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), particularly when utilizing events with one top quark and one jet. By comparing next-to-leading-order (NLO) and next-to-next-to-leading-order (NNLO) QCD predictions for single-top production in the presence of an extra jet, the impact of off-shell corrections on m_t is found to be significant, amounting to approximately 10% to 20% in the NLO case. A dedicated analysis of ttj events at the LHC is then performed using a parton-level event generator, revealing that incorporating off-shell contributions boosts the precision of m_t by up to 20% to 30%. Furthermore, the study shows that combining data from both the 13 TeV and 8 TeV LHC leads to a m_t value of 172.49 GeV, with a corresponding theoretical uncertainty of 0.58 GeV.

Recent advancements in using deep convolutional neural networks for face anti-spoofing tasks have led to significant performance improvements. A specific area known as zero-shot face anti-spoofing, where templates are not required for classification, has garnered increasing interest. The limited capacity of traditional convolutional neural networks in handling complex data led to the introduction of transformer models, particularly vision transformers, in computer vision tasks. This research investigates the effectiveness of using vision transformers in zero-shot face anti-spoofing, and to the best of our knowledge, this is the first time such an approach has been explored. The findings reveal that vision transformers outperform conventional approaches, demonstrating better performance on public datasets.

Deep reinforcement learning stands out as a promising AI paradigm for instructing machines via environmental interaction and adaptive learning from their mistakes. Its potential in autonomous driving has garnered significant attention, given the challenges inherent in traditional approaches. Deep reinforcement learning can address complex problems like object interaction and environment optimization, and its application in autonomous driving has shown promise in simulations and on-road trials. However, deep reinforcement learning still requires substantial improvements in real-world capability and environmental understanding. Our research aims to provide an in-depth review of the most effective deep reinforcement learning methods in the context of autonomous driving, along with a review of the most prevalent simulation tools utilized in the field. Furthermore, we will discuss the current hurdles in deploying these algorithms in real-world settings and suggest potential solutions for further investigation.

Evolutionary algorithms have been widely utilized for complex multi-objective optimization problems, and recent advancements in parallel computing have led to the development of parallel MOPSAAs to significantly decrease the overall computation time. However, the uneven processing time of individuals by the evaluator causes asynchronous Parent-Offspring selection methods to produce biased results. This paper introduces an innovative parent selection method, utilizing the frequency of each parent's selection instead of the processing time of the candidates. The proposed selection method is then evaluated on three multi-objective test problems and compared to the II parent selection method, which is known to mitigate evaluation time bias. The experimental outcomes demonstrate that the proposed selection method is not only free from evaluation time bias but also effectively reduces the variability of computation time, and ultimately achieves higher convergence results without increasing the average computation time.

We develop effective, time-independent master equations that approximate the behavior of open quantum systems under rapid, periodic transformations, which are crucial in quantum computing and quantum information processing. Our approach is grounded in a mathematical framework that describes how these systems change over time, using a linear operator to track the evolution of key properties. By analyzing the operator's behavior, we can derive both high-frequency and systematic expansion formulas for the operator's approximation, which enables us to derive similar formulas for key performance metrics in quantum information processing. Our main findings include the derivation of an effective, time-independent master equation for open quantum systems that undergo rapid, periodic transformations, as well as a mathematical expression for the operator that governs the evolution of these systems. Our approach is validated by examining a model quantum processor based on superconducting circuits, which we use to calculate the effective noise operator that governs the evolution of a quantum memory element under rapid, periodic changes. Our results demonstrate that high-frequency expansion correctly predicts the behavior of this element, which is essential for accurate quantum computing.

Researchers have found that the way neighboring atomic magnetic moments interact directly affects how they slow down and organize themselves as temperature decreases. In the current study, the relationship between the presence of a ferromagnetic phase transition and the onset of spin freezing in the CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ series was investigated through the analysis of both long-range ferromagnetism and short-range correlations in the material. By using time-of-flight neutron-scattering experiments, the team discovered that the long-range ferromagnetism in CePdRh and CeFePd results in the loss of polarization of neutrons before they reach their detectors. On the other hand, the same phenomenon was found to occur at lower temperatures in samples without long-range ferromagnetism, indicating spin freezing. These results were further supported by the findings of muon spin relaxation measurements, which showed that the loss of polarization in these samples occurs at different rates. These results were also found to be consistent with the team's previous findings on similar materials.

In deep neural network training, access to extensive, labeled datasets is often unobtainable, and usual methods fail to yield optimal results when applied to unfamiliar datasets. The issue is particularly prevalent in cases where datasets differ significantly, either in terms of their distribution or the types of data they contain. The challenge is addressed by a class-oblivious domain adaptation process, which aims to adapt a pre-trained model, initially developed using a dataset's features, for use on another, dissimilar dataset. The objective is to enhance the model's performance on the new dataset without altering its core architecture. A variety of domain adaptation techniques have been proposed to tackle this problem. The techniques differ in the extent to which they modify the model, ranging from minimal adjustments to complete reinitialization. The techniques also vary in the type of information they utilize, including features, gradients, and outputs, and can be further categorized as methods that incorporate external datasets, those that utilize self-learning techniques, and those that rely on optimization methods. The performance of these techniques has been extensively evaluated, and the results indicate that the best outcomes are typically achieved by techniques that incorporate significant modifications and utilize features, gradients, and outputs interchangeably.

A pictorial proof shows that there are $\binom{n+2}{4}$ equilateral triangles in a regular $n$-sided triangle by establishing a one-to-one correspondence between four-element subsets of the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n+2\}$ and the equilateral triangles in this grid, where it is visually represented by marking the vertices of the triangles in a diagram illustrating the relationship between the triangle's grid and the number line.

Despite recent advancements in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), their lack of transparency and interpretability has hindered their adoption in high-stakes applications. To address this issue, we have developed an innovative approach to interpret GNN predictions by incrementally removing influential graph structures, parameterized by a heat map. By utilizing our novel Edge Influence Score (EIS) metric, which subsumes existing measures, we have established a comprehensive framework for interpreting GNNs. Through rigorous testing on five real-world datasets, we have demonstrated the superior performance of our method in understanding GNN models, outperforming existing benchmarks.

The galaxy cluster RXCJ0232.2-4420, located at redshift z=0.28, was observed using the Chandra X-ray telescope. This led to a detailed analysis of its global parameters and substructure. By examining X-ray surface brightness and pressure maps, we determined the cluster's distance and orientation within the sky. Furthermore, we calculated its temperature, X-ray luminosity, and hydrostatic mass. The results showed that the cluster's temperature was consistent across different regions, suggesting that it is in thermal equilibrium. The cluster's X-ray luminosity was estimated based on the temperature and hydrostatic mass. The analysis of the gas distribution revealed that the cluster is not in hydrostatic equilibrium due to the presence of two distinct regions with different pressure values. The cluster's distance and orientation were confirmed through the examination of nearby radio sources.

Recently, the Legendre Memory Unit (LMU), a novel type of recurrent neural network, was introduced and has demonstrated exceptional performance on various benchmark datasets. In this study, we delve into the specifics of the LMU architecture and training methodology in order to enhance its scalability. Our findings reveal that the traditional Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) optimizer utilized in the original implementation is suboptimal. We have discovered that SGD tends to converge prematurely due to inadequate parameter updates. To address this shortcoming, we have successfully integrated the Adam optimizer into the LMU training routine. Our proposed parallelized implementation of the LMU with Adam optimizer (PAR-LMU) has been benchmarked against the conventional setup in multiple experiments. Notably, the PAR-LMU model exhibited a marked increase in training convergence, and more importantly, its accuracy on specific datasets can be fine-tuned via adversarial training using the Adam optimizer.

As the next decade unfolds, the high-energy physics community is poised to take a significant step forward in exploring new and innovative frontiers. One of the most promising areas of research is the quest to detect particles with feebly-interacting forces, represented by models like the Lee-Warner-Yeomans and the "Simplified" FIP models. This research paper provides an in-depth examination of the theoretical foundation behind feebly-interacting particles, followed by an exhaustive analysis of the most effective and suitable experimental approaches for uncovering them. The report is a collaborative effort between the ILC, LHC, and beyond-LEP III working groups and is informed by the 2020 CERN Physics Report, with significant additions and updates.

Language development among groups of individuals is studied using a complex network simulation. The naming game simulation yields significant, predictable outcomes when agents are free to move within the network. When multiple stable languages coexist, limited interactions between groups tend to drive language convergence, ultimately leading to uniform communication. Our research reveals that this uniform outcome can occur through two distinct mechanisms, one being the common randomization process that occurs when multiple languages coexist. Interestingly, a second mechanism involves the migration of agents and subsequent local interactions, resulting in consistent outcomes regardless of the initial network setup. These findings align with prior research on language development, supporting the idea that migration and movement play a crucial role in shaping language patterns.

PINN training often faces challenges due to the combination of two conflicting objectives: achieving a good fit of the network with limited data, and satisfying the boundary conditions with high accuracy. One of the primary obstacles hindering PINN convergence is the issue of spectral bias, which causes networks with different architectures but using the same activation function to converge to varying solutions based solely on their architecture. A study has been conducted to investigate the impact of using stochastic gradient descent with momentum on PINN model convergence. By utilizing a range of activation functions, including the traditional ReLU, the alternative soft ReLU, and the sublinear ReLU, the experiments showed that incorporating momentum into the optimization process significantly diminishes the effects of spectral bias, with the sublinear ReLU activation function producing solutions similar to those produced by ReLU and soft ReLU, which are within a factor of 10 of each other in terms of L2 loss.

We examine a two-wave system in the interval (-1,1), where one wave absorbs energy and the other does not, with partial damping that mimics a viscoelastic material's behavior. Prior research showed that with damping throughout the entire domain, the system's energy decreases at a rate proportional to $t^{-\frac{1}{2}}$. Using the frequency domain method in this paper, we show the system's behavior changes significantly due to the waves being coupled and the non-smooth damping coefficient, specifically that the system's energy decreases at a rate proportional to $t^{-\frac{1}{4}}$.

Recent advances in deep reinforcement learning have led to widespread applications of autonomous agents, but the complexity of the learned policies hinders their transparency.  This problem is addressed by a new framework called HiRL-IL, which enables hierarchical reinforcement learning at multiple skill levels while providing a clear understanding of each skill.  Our approach involves using an Inductive Logic Programming model to define high-level skills as conditional statements, allowing for easy interpretation.  This method also incorporates a mechanism to transfer knowledge to subsequent skill levels through experience sharing.  Our framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through its successful application in a simulated robotic task, where it successfully acquired multiple skills with varying levels of complexity.  Notably, the high-level skills learned by HiRL-IL in this experiment closely resemble the underlying motion primitives predicted by motion planning algorithms, showcasing the model's high fidelity and transparency.

We've developed an all-optical technique for producing optical nonreciprocity on a microscale, achieved through the process of quantum squeezing. By leveraging an optomechanical system with nonlinear loss and driven by a pump, we show that only the forward-traveling field experiences quantum squeezing, leading to optical nonreciprocity. The method was tested using both numerical simulations and real-world experiments, demonstrating that nonreciprocity can occur even at low input powers and confirming that the method operates primarily through quantum squeezing rather than by increasing the gain's phase.

This research investigates a specific class of functionals derived from the translation of sum functions and defined on a compact set. Our study focuses on the existence and characteristics of their minimax problems with constraints, building upon MacKay and Potts' initial work and expanding it to include various types of sets and functionals. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for functional anti-aggregation for a broader range of input data, and demonstrate that under certain assumptions, the minimax problem has a solution that can be expressed as a maximin problem. Specifically, under specific hypotheses, the minimax solution can be expressed as a maximin problem whose objective function is based on a weighted sum of the original functions, where the weights are determined by the data corresponding to the minimax problem.

The CRESST experiment has a key role to play in investigating spin-dependent interactions between dark matter and nuclei.  By analyzing thulium-doped calcium tungstate crystals used in the experiment's calorimeters, researchers can study the direct detection of dark matter interactions.  The research discussed focuses on revised measurements of the two-component nuclear response and of the ¹H and ²H quasi-elastic cross-sections essential for data analysis.  The new results significantly reduce uncertainties in the calculation of the recoil rates, leading to a revised 90% confidence level sensitivity limit of 2.0*10^-17 ergs/cm²/keVs for spin-dependent interactions involving 40-kilogram targets and a 25-kiloelectronvolt threshold.  The new measurements also enable the investigation of spin-dependent interactions involving which can be probed with a 90% confidence level sensitivity limit of 2.5*10^-17 ergs/cm²/keVs in the case of ²H.

Blind Image deblurring attempts to estimate a latent sharp image and the blur kernel that created it, given only the blurred image. The conventional approach of calculating the blur kernel directly from the blurred image is hindered by its low resolution and irregular shape. This paper introduces a novel method that models the blur kernel as a mixture of Gaussian kernels, reducing the kernel estimation to a process of identifying the mixture model parameters. The framework is based on the Hidden Markov Model, where the hidden state represents the type of Gaussian kernel and the corresponding mean and variance. The EM algorithm is used to estimate the parameters, where the responsibility of each hidden state determines the local gradient and noise of the image patch, guiding the sharp image estimation. The performance of this method is demonstrated through experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, showcasing its ability to accurately recover details, especially in areas with similar textures.

This paper introduces a concept of homogeneous and non-homogeneous associative Yang-Baxter (AYB) equations, representing two distinct forms of structural equations in the context of quasi-Hopf algebras and their related bi-modules. The study focuses on solving the non-homogeneous AYB equation, given that a solution exists for its homogeneous counterpart. The paper also defines and explores the concept of non-homogeneous AYB equation's'support'. Furthermore, it establishes a link between solutions to the non-homogeneous AYB equation and 'extra' linear maps between bi-modules, particularly when the non-homogeneous solution's support is confined to a single module.

A groundbreaking verification method, known as Natural Hoare Logic, is proposed to formalize specifications in a form of Hoare logic that mirrors the structure of natural language. This approach is distinguished from existing formal verification techniques by its ability to leverage natural language descriptions, rather than formal mathematical formulas. We establish a framework for translating natural language requirements into a well-defined form of Hoare logic using semantic interpretation. This technique is demonstrated on a selection of programs, including a version of QuickSort, to showcase its efficacy. Furthermore, we examine the advantages of our method, particularly its capacity to utilize natural language to articulate preconditions, postconditions, and invariants, and its ability to generate explicit program Hoare specifications through reverse engineering.

Distributed consensus is a fundamental concept, with many consensus algorithms, such as PBFT and Raft, being widely used across various distributed systems. These protocols, however, are generally designed to handle failures that are not malicious in nature. This study introduces RCanopus, an enhanced version of the Canopus consensus algorithm that not only tolerates failure-induced disruptions but also withstands the influence of malicious Byzantine faults. By incorporating a novel approach, specifically the use of a composite failure detection mechanism, combining explicit failure detection with implicit failure assumption relaxation, RCanopus achieves resilience against a range of failure types. Experimental evaluations using a 100 node cluster demonstrate that RCanopus is capable of withstanding up to 33 Byzantine faults while maintaining performance efficiency.

Recent studies utilizing the flaccid liposome method have yielded a wide range of values for the bending modulus of lipid bilayers, spanning across three decimal places. We aim to resolve discrepancies between research findings by employing a systematic approach to analyze the impact of model assumptions. Our analysis focuses on the effect of cholesterol on the bending modulus, revealing that certain model assumptions can result in a significant variation of 30% in the measured parameter. We also introduce a novel expression for the effective bending modulus in a two-component lipid blend and derive conditions under which this parameter can be treated as an additive property.

This study presents a novel Loop Quantum Cosmological Model derived directly from the ADM Hamiltonian. It shows that the Hamiltonian can be rewritten in an equivalent form with a potential representing an effective mass. By applying the Loop Quantum Graphity Approach, the quantum representation of the redefined Hamiltonian leads to a new LQC model where the effective mass serves as a cosmological constant. This model's underlying structure is investigated, and it is found that the scaling LQC model's physical states transition into a new base state in the effective LQC model. Furthermore, the new LQC model exhibits an inverse scaling behavior, where the volume of the universe increases as the average arm length grows, and the scaling exponents converge to zero.

The Pierre Auger Observatory catalog details 100 extensive air-showers recorded over nine years, covering the highest-energy range of 8 to 60 EeV. This catalog supplements the observatory's research dataset and offers a resource for cross-checking with other cosmic ray experiments, including the newly operational IceTop detector at the Pierre Augin Collider and the highly sensitive and accurate POEMMA satellite-based experiment, set to collect data in the near future. This experiment is a collaborative effort between the Department of Nuclear Engineering at the University of Michigan and the Russian Institute for Nuclear Research.

Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success in object detection tasks, but their reliability for real-world applications remains uncertain due to incomplete knowledge of error rates. Conventional methods for object detection based on maximum likelihood optimization overlook their mistakes, while existing uncertainty estimates are generally task-specific or unreliable. A novel approach called BayesOD has been developed to provide a general and accurate uncertainty measure for object detectors. By reinterpreting the network's output as a posterior probability, BayesOD estimates the uncertainty of object predictions. This uncertainty is calculated using an innovative method that outperforms traditional techniques. BayesOD can be integrated into existing object detectors without modifications to their architecture or parameters. When applied to Faster R-CNN and RetinaNet, BayesOD demonstrates superior performance, outperforming other uncertainty estimation methods.

In traffic forecasting, predicting the movement of traffic particles from a limited observation period can significantly benefit road network management and operation. This study introduces a new traffic forecasting framework, called TrafficNet, which utilizes a specific type of neural network called graph convolutional network to process data collected from moving traffic particles. By continuously updating predictions based on evolving network structures, TrafficNet can adapt to changing road conditions. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of TrafficNet in outperforming baseline models, even under limited data conditions.

In recent years, rewriting theory has been extended to cover algebraic structures more broadly, including categories like bidirectional categories and Gray categories. This study takes rewriting theory to the next level by applying it to Gray categories, a specific type of braided monoidal category. To achieve this, the concept of commutativity is integrated into rewriting rules, allowing for the interpretation of these rules in the Gray category's symmetries. Two key methods are developed for creating rewriting systems in Gray categories, one involving the translation of existing systems from lower-level structures and the other serving as a general construction for creating coherent rewriting systems. This research demonstrates the potential of rewriting theory by showing its applications in proving coherence for example Gray categories, including categories for clonotopy, clustergroups, and monoidal double categories.

Automatically segmenting the hippocampi from magnetic resonance imaging is crucial for diagnosing and treating neurological disorders, including epilepsy and Alzheimer's disease. In this paper, we evaluate the performance of several convolutional neural networks on hippocampi segmentation tasks from two datasets collected from patients with epilepsy and Alzheimer's disease. The networks assessed were U-Net, ResNet, GoogLeNet, and FractalNet, all of which were trained on hippocampi segmentation tasks from the epilepsy dataset before being tested on the Alzheimer's dataset. The results showed that the U-Net and ResNet performed better than the other networks, achieving Dice scores of 0.90 and 0.88, respectively, on the Alzheimer's dataset. Notably, using the epilepsy dataset for training yielded better performance than cross-dataset training, highlighting the potential of transfer learning in hippocampi segmentation tasks.

We examine the phenomenon of the pigeonhole effect, a consequence of STIRAP-like transfer of coherence from a more energetic to a less energetic state, where the interference pattern between the two final states is more complex due to the additional modes participating in the process. In the case of two final states, the interference pattern reflects the relative population of the two states, but with multiple excited states involved, the interference pattern is modified by the contribution of these additional states, resulting in changes to the pattern's phase. Our analysis reveals that the phase shift can be tied to the specific number of excited states and the direction of population transfer between the two primary states, providing new avenues for investigating the pigeonhole effect.

Our research reveals that cosmic ray albedo neutrons and protons in the Earth's magnetic field can be trapped not only at geosynchronous orbit but also at lower altitudes, including those below 1000 km. We employed Geant4 Monte Carlo simulations to investigate the generation of protons through the CRAND process at the low Earth orbit of the SWARM-A satellite. The results show that the integrated proton flux at this altitude is 10^7 protons per square centimeter per second, which is equivalent to 10^4 particles per second hitting the SWARM-A instrument. These protons contribute to instrument background noise and error, particularly in the magnetic field measurement, which could reach up to 1 ngal per second.

In recent years, Deep Graph Neural Networks have garnered significant attention, 
thanks to their ability to tackle complex graph-related tasks. However, their 
performance is often limited by their inherent difficulties in processing node 
representations and making informed decision-making. To address these challenges, 
we propose a novel architecture design that leverages node pyramid networks 
and link reconfiguration. Specifically, we suggest capturing node features at 
different scales, and then using these features to construct a structured 
framework. Furthermore, we propose local topology adaptation to refine node 
interactions and improve network communication. Our architecture's effectiveness 
is demonstrated through experiments on multiple benchmark datasets, where it 
significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in semi-supervised node 
classification tasks.

This paper presents an efficient technique for privately filling in missing entries of a partially observed low-dimensional matrix, given access to a closely related fully observed matrix. The proposed method minimizes the difference between the two matrices using a form of the Huber loss function, which has been used in statistical contexts. The development of this method leverages the insight that combining multiple related datasets can lead to more accurate completions. The method's privacy properties are ensured through a novel application of the differential privacy framework to a process involving sampling and adding noise to entries. The approach is evaluated using synthetic data and comparisons with other completion methods demonstrate its effectiveness in low-dimensional settings.

A new model for interstellar dust has been developed, combining the effects of small dust particles and larger grains. Research suggests that these dust particles are primarily composed of carbon and oxygen, while larger grains are primarily made up of silicates. When these dust particles are heated by starlight, they emit energy in the form of infrared light within a specific timeframe, typically on a scale of 10 to 100 years. This phenomenon is a critical factor in understanding how starlight interacts with space due to the absorption and scattering of light by interstellar dust, which in turn affects our view of the cosmos. This model has been applied to a specific type of emission, PAH emission, which is a key component of this process. This type of emission is a result of the excitation of small carbon-based molecules when radiation from nearby stars interacts with interstellar dust. This model has been applied to a specific type of starlight interactions, but it can be used to study other types of astronomical phenomena.

The study of extrasolar planets in relation to their parent star's mass is still in its early stages, particularly in cases where the parent star has a low mass. This research aims to fill this gap by conducting a comprehensive analysis of the planetary system around CIDA 1, a low-mass star located at the center of a protoplanetary disk. Using ALMA's sensitive observations, the team was able to map the distribution of dust and gas in the disk and identify distinct substructures. They discovered two areas of increased dust concentration, one of which could be explained by the presence of a superheated inner region. However, the second region appeared to be a gap of at least 10 times deeper than the surrounding dust levels, suggesting it was caused by a massive planetary object. Using a planetary model, the team estimated the mass of the planetary object to be around 10-15 M_J, assuming an orbital radius of 0.1 AU. This finding has significant implications for the understanding of planetary formation and migration, particularly in cases where the parent star has a low mass.

Consider the rules of a popular light-switching game played on a simple graph with fully connected nodes: (1) a light on a node can be turned off but not the other way around, (2) a light is turned off by switching the node it's on, (3) a light is turned on by switching the node it's off on. The goal is to create a sequence of switchings that turns all lights off, but the sequence must be determined without looking ahead, meaning each switching can only depend on the current state of the lights. A recent study showed this problem is solvable for any initial graph state if the number of nodes is finite. However, the study left open the question of finding the best strategy for the problem, specifically which sequence of switchings maximizes the number of clicks required to solve it. In this paper, we provide a solution to this question: the optimal strategy is a sequence that turns off as many lights as possible in the fewest number of clickings, which can be achieved by solving a combinatorial problem known as the maximum independent set problem in graphs.

This paper presents a novel, multi-stage image segmentation model that integrates image restoration techniques to improve the performance of standard variational image segmentation models, particularly when dealing with low-quality input images. Classical image segmentation models are often sensitive to noise and other image imperfections, but our approach demonstrates that by removing these imperfections through image restoration techniques, the quality of the segmentation results can be significantly enhanced. To achieve this, we propose a model that simultaneously performs image restoration and segmentation using a modified variational image segmentation model tailored for degraded input images, and our experimental results confirm the superiority of our approach compared to traditional methods.

Program analysis through Abstract Interpretation involves simulating the behavior of a program in a simplified environment to approximate its true behavior. This simulation traditionally has two steps: the ascending phase, which calculates the program's reachability set, and the descending phase, which interprets the results by applying a fixpoint computation over that set. However, these steps are inherently connected and, in current approaches, it is unclear when and how they should be executed. This paper proposes a new framework, called the DA framework, that allows the ascending and descending phases to run independently and makes the choice of their order and interaction with each other flexible. The DA framework also introduces a new concept, called the abstract flow, that facilitates the interaction between these phases by defining how values are updated during the analysis. The framework is formalized and its benefits are demonstrated through a simple case study, showing how different scheduling strategies can improve the efficiency of the analysis.

We investigate theoretically the impact of light on the topological phonons in 
perovskite crystals, specifically LaAlO$_3$ and BaTiO$_3$, which are crucial for 
photonic applications and exhibit complex dynamics when interacted with light. 
Using time-dependent density functional perturbation theory, our results show that 
light induces significant changes in the phonon structure, leading to the 
creation of secondary topological states, and altering the original topological 
states by shifting their frequencies. Furthermore, our results indicate that the 
light-induced topological states can be controlled by varying the frequency and 
polarization of the laser used, and that these states may persist even after the 
laser is turned off, suggesting potential for stable topological phonics in 
perovskite crystals.

Detecting irregularities in data is crucial for various applications, including fraud detection and anomaly-based intrusion detection.
The process of identifying irregularities in large datasets can be computationally intensive due to the time-consuming process of searching for anomalies under certain conditions.
To address this challenge, researchers have developed more efficient algorithms for detecting irregularities in data.
A novel method, referred to as FastOD, leverages graph algorithms and query optimization to rapidly identify irregularities in data organized into clusters.
FastOD employs a specialized graph structure to map data to nearest neighbors and identify anomalies based on their proximity to the cluster center.
A key innovation in FastOD involves query optimization techniques that enable efficient processing of queries using secondary indexes.
FastOD's performance is further enhanced by the use of caching techniques and query simplification methods.
Experimental results demonstrate that FastOD is significantly faster than traditional methods, especially for large datasets and complex queries.
Notably, FastOD is designed to support parallel processing, making it suitable for execution on large datasets with multiple threads.

The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is analyzed for a non-relativistic, two-state atom interacting with a quantum electromagnetic field reflected off a perfectly conducting plane under conditions where the atom is initially at rest and subsequently very close to the mirror. It's discovered that when the atom is driven towards the mirror, not only does its kinetic energy change, but its (de-)excitation probability and emitted photons also vary significantly from the results obtained using the Foldy-Feynman formalism, especially at high velocities. Conversely, when the mirror is moved towards a stationary atom, the results show a high probability of excitation and photon emission, even at low velocities, and the emitted spectrum deviates from the results obtained using the Foldy-Feynman formalism, especially at low frequencies.

As the importance of Graph Neural Networks grows within the machine learning community, the need to adapt existing models to changing data becomes more significant. Most graph data structures rely on a close relationship between a node's features and its surrounding neighborhood. However, conventional fairness metrics fail to account for the complex relationships in graph-structured data. This study proposes a novel fairness metric called Localized Neighborhood Fairness, capturing the nuanced characteristics of neighborhood connections while considering individual node attributes. A regulatory mechanism is introduced to weigh the influence of different neighborhoods, allowing for flexible customization of the metric. A comprehensive theoretical framework is developed to analyze the fairness metric's properties, and numerical experiments demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in graph learning with localized neighborhood fairness.

This paper examines kinetic models for reversible enzyme reactions and evaluates the effectiveness of two analytical techniques in reducing computational complexity: the Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel iteration methods. These methods apply to a broad class of nonlinear Almond equations, which describe reversible enzyme reactions. The analysis reveals that the Jacobi iteration method can reduce the 2n-degree polynomial nonlinearity of the Almond equation to (2n/2)+1 or 2n-degree polynomial nonlinearity for each of the n subsystems. In contrast, the Gauss-Seidel iteration method yields a lower degree of nonlinearity for each subsystem: (n+1), 2n-3, n-2, and n degrees of polynomial for the four possible ranges of the parameter m. However, the analysis indicates that the accuracy of the Gauss-Seidel method depends on specific values of the parameter m. The study also reveals that the Almond equation can be further simplified into a system of quadratic equations under the condition m=2.

A search for supersymmetry is conducted in proton-proton collisions produced by the LHC, utilizing data from a 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ dataset. The search targets strong production of supersymmetric particles, focusing on final states featuring high-energy jets and significant missing transverse momentum. To distinguish between various potential decay modes of neutralinos, a classification system is employed, prioritizing regions with multiple jets over those with a $W$ or a top quark, and further separating them by the presence of up to three jets. In regions with the smallest number of jets, sensitivity to gluino-mediated squark production is enhanced through the application of an enhanced jet veto. In regions with the largest number of jets, sensitivity to squark production is primarily at the squark mass level. No significant excess is found, and the results are interpreted through the creation of squark pairs ($\sqrt{s}$) and strong production of gluinos with masses up to 1.4 TeV. The results are also applied to split supersymmetry scenarios, focusing on the lightest visible particle, assumed to be a gravitino, and setting limits on the mass of the decaying neutralino at masses up to 460 GeV.

Two proposed expectation models for temporary financial bubbles, characterized by agents' rational expectations and limited market information, have been introduced recently.  This paper develops new diagnostic tests and provides evidence on the preference models' validity using daily data on stock prices in Japan and Germany from 1989 to 2019.  The first test identifies bubble presence by checking for unusual price changes, while the second assesses the likelihood of each model given observed price paths.  Our analysis indicates that bubble occurrence is evident in both markets, supporting the limited market information model.  Furthermore, we estimate the expected termination times of these bubbles and find them consistent with their theoretical nature as random variables having a Weibull distribution.

Quantum harmonic oscillators are being investigated using a Markov chain Monte Carlo approach to both steady and time-varying conditions. The effects of temperature are also being considered. To simulate the behavior of these oscillators, a specific type of molecular dynamics simulation is employed, which accounts for quantum behavior. This method's primary goal is to verify previously published findings on the equilibrium properties of an oscillator subjected to strong driving. To achieve this, a detailed explanation of the underlying theoretical framework is provided, followed by a comparison between the analytical solution and the simulation results for both the equilibrium and time-varying conditions.

Recent research has shown that user-item interaction matrices can effectively capture the complexities of user preferences. However, current recommendation models are limited in their ability to analyze reviews holistically, failing to utilize the rich information content, sentiment, and semantic relationships within. To address this, a new approach is proposed, consisting of a Sentiment-aware Interactive Fusion Network that integrates reviews at both the sentence and sentence-level, leveraging external knowledge sources to enhance understanding. The model's ability to determine relevance is demonstrated through a novel task involving review matching, and experiments on real-world datasets reveal its superiority in precision and recall over established baselines.

Developing CS NLP systems is challenging due to the scarcity of CS data and resources available for Arabic-English, a language pair that is becoming increasingly popular in various regions. This study aims to improve data augmentation using various lexical replacement techniques to produce high-quality CS text. We compare these methods with state-of-the-art word-level masking algorithms and assess their effectiveness in enhancing CS NLP performance. Notably, our findings indicate that employing multiple lexical replacement sequences to generate multiple augmented sequences leads to superior results, outperforming a leading word-level model. This research also sheds light on potential errors in data augmentation caused by replacement methods.

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the compactly generated topological category, is not relatively compact according to the Leibman topology, has unbounded distortion. Similarly, any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a non-orientable surface that also fix the boundary, exhibiting a similar subgroup structure, also demonstrates extreme distortion. This finding stands in contrast to subgroups of surface homeomorphisms that fix the boundary and are relatively compact according to the Leibman topology, which were previously studied by Matucci and Golan, Brech, and Kechris.

We have investigated integrable boundary conditions, or branes, within specific theoretical models, including a $SU(2)$-based generalized lambda deformation and an $SO(1,2)$-based de Sitter k-Poincare non-compact dual. Our analysis led to a systematic characterization of boundary conditions compatible with these modified theories. We discovered that certain boundary conditions previously known to be compatible with the underlying CFTs continued to be invariant under the lambda deformation, providing a geometric framework to establish the equivalence between the two theories. Additionally, our work has yielded new insights into the properties of Gaudin models and free fermions when adapted to the deformed frameworks.

Hex mesh topology offers the most efficient data structure for a wide range of simulations, but its rigid structure also makes it prone to severe distortion. As a result, complex geometries often require a large number of hex elements, which can lead to an excessive number of costly nodes to be solved for in optimization or simulation. To mitigate this issue, a novel approach has been developed, utilizing a highly efficient data structure to support complex topologies with a minimal number of nodes. By leveraging advanced algorithms, this method can support up to 58 tets per hex element, allowing a significant reduction in the total number of nodes required. To achieve this, a custom data structure has been designed with optimized node ordering, enabling efficient access and operations. Furthermore, a comprehensive set of algorithms has been implemented to support a wide range of applications, including linear solver, mesh copy, and surface access. To facilitate efficient data exchange, interfaces have been established with popular libraries, such as VTK and PETSc. A comprehensive suite of tests has been developed to validate the robustness and performance of this approach, demonstrating its ability to handle complex topologies with up to 58 tets per hex element, while achieving comparable or better performance than existing solutions, including FEniCS, PETSc, and VTK.

A crucial task in natural language processing, relation extraction is used to establish connections between entities in a sentence, with applications extending to knowledge graph construction, semantic search, and information retrieval, among other benefits, however, the process is often hindered by data scarcity issues, particularly the shortage of training data, with models struggling to generalize and perform well in new scenarios, our research aims to mitigate this challenge by drawing from pre-existing knowledge graphs, specifically by utilizing knowledge graph link prediction models to generate additional relation assertions, with these generated assertions then utilized in relation extraction, the efficacy of this integrated approach was tested on several datasets, with results indicating a significant boost in performance, with the combined method outperforming the baseline by an average margin of 4.8%, with notable improvements observed in datasets previously thought to be data-sufficient, the code utilized in this research has been made publicly available on the GitHub platform.

This research introduces an innovative analytical delay model specifically tailored for deep submicron CMOS inverters. Developed using a data-driven approach, it employs a combination of user-defined functional components via the Curve Fitting Toolbox in Matlab.
