To demonstrate its effectiveness, the model exhibits high precision in predicting inverter delay with minimal error, showing an average discrepancy of less than 1% compared to SPICE simulations for a wide range of process variants. Moreover, the model's computational complexity is remarkably low, requiring only 12 parameters to capture the intricate behavior of inverter delay across diverse CMOS technologies. As a result, the proposed analytical delay model holds significant promise for users of static CMOS process design flows to accelerate inverter-based circuit design optimization and verification.

We've developed a way to create a broad, general class of reinforcement learning techniques that work in any metric space. Our approach is inspired by the principle that in a new, unfamiliar environment, it's often better to explore the most interesting options, rather than delving into the most comfortable ones. This is based on a mathematical concept called coarse smoothness, which we've adapted from optimization theory to create our RL framework. By using this framework, we've demonstrated that we can replicate the performance of the most advanced reinforcement learning algorithms, all within a metric space.

The ability to distinguish living things is a fundamental aspect of human cognition, evident from recognizing a face to perceiving a predator at a distance. While research has shown that animacy can be identified across various domains, the neural mechanisms underlying this ability remain unclear. Specifically, it is not known whether a specialized network exists that governs animacy perception. To investigate this question, a study using functional magnetic resonance imaging across different levels of animacy complexity was conducted, which revealed a network involving the lateral and medial fusiform gyri. This discovery suggests that a dedicated system exists to organize animacy perception, which is further supported by evidence of a network's stability across varying levels of complexity.

A novel, high-order finite element filter has been proposed for large-scale simulations performed using the finite element method. This innovative filter design, grounded in convex optimization, ensures the preservation of positive material properties and energy stability, while maintaining a low computational cost. Numerical experiments conducted using 2D and 3D models demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed filter, which successfully maintains the accuracy of solutions at both smooth and discontinuous points without compromising numerical stability.

The study of a superluminal pulsar, MAXI J1535-571, has been significant due to its unique characteristics. Researchers have investigated the evolution of its corona surrounding the accretion disk using data from the Insight-HXMT satellite. By analyzing the spectrum and time-dependent data, they identified type-C quasi-periodic oscillations and their connections to the corona's size. A notable finding was that the corona's size increased as the system transitioned from a high and soft state to a low and hard state. This correlation was further supported by the use of a Comptonization model, and it also aligns with expectations based on the balance between the disk's radiation and the corona's heating.

In the context of multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly for tasks requiring cooperation and communication, our proposed Social Intrinsic Motivation (SIM) framework addresses the issue of agents being detached from their environment. We introduce transfer empowerment as a key concept, enabling agents to assess their influence on other agents and vice versa. This framework has two components: environment empowerment, which encourages exploration of the physical world, and interaction empowerment, which encourages effective communication and cooperation with other agents. We test the SIM framework in a cooperative task, where two agents need to communicate to achieve a common goal, and find that incorporating interaction empowerment results in improved performance and more efficient use of bandwidth by avoiding unnecessary messages. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the interaction empowerment signal can be utilized as a means of measuring the complexity of communication within the system.

Our proposed method employs contrastive learning to recognize any material, 
regardless of the reference image, by utilizing a simulator to generate 
synthetic images based on a material's properties. This allows the model to 
determine a material's identity solely by looking at two images, without 
requiring prior knowledge and as a single, self-supervised input. This is 
achieved through a material's inherent structural consistency, which serves as 
a visual anchor for the model to rely on. Our experiments demonstrate that 
this approach surpasses baselines in performance and provide a comprehensive 
understanding of the method's workings through ablation studies and 
interrogative analysis. This research has practical implications for real-world 
applications, as we successfully test the method on a dataset comprising 
materials found in everyday environments.

Two equivalent definitions of Lie 2-algebras are recalled, along with selected examples. A detailed overview is provided of four types of homomorphisms between Lie 2-algebras, accompanied by relevant applications and discussions. Notably, cross connections with Poincaré-Birkhoff-Witt theorems in higher Lie algebras are touched upon.

We introduce LoFTR, a novel detector-free local feature matching approach, where we leverage multiple detectors to cover the entire image at different scales to extract dense local features. Unlike traditional methods that rely on hand-crafted low-level features and intricate geometric structures to compute pixel-wise correspondences, LoFTR employs self-attention mechanisms to align scale-aware local features across images. By localizing correspondences through a cross-patch matching process guided by non-local feature affinity, LoFTR achieves dense correspondence estimation at a fraction of the cost of traditional methods. Our results demonstrate that-loop self-supervised learning can refine the feature representation of even high-quality detectors to facilitate accurate correspondence computation. By integrating LoFTR's dense correspondences with different 3D reconstruction pipelines, we have achieved state-of-the-art results on challenging benchmarks, including 3D Carla scenarios, 3D KITTI, TUM-MSR, and ETH-RGBD tracks.

The study of the Sun's corona and its underlying processes relies heavily on vector magnetic field data, which is often derived from solar images taken with various telescopes. However, the different observational capabilities of these telescopes can lead to discrepancies in data, particularly when comparing data collected using different instruments. To address this issue, we have developed a new approach to identify potential biases in solar physics research. Specifically, we have created metrics to quantify the consistency of vector magnetic field data derived from different observatories. Through statistical analysis, we have found that the data from the New Vacuum Solar Telescope and the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph exhibit significant discrepancies in spatial distribution, suggesting the presence of bias. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that the bias can be mitigated by applying a data weighting scheme based on our developed metrics, which ultimately enhances the overall reliability of the data.

This research paper explores a novel concept of Autonomous Demand Side Management (ASDM) that relies on an understanding of energy consumption scheduling and real-time billing. We've developed an ASDM framework that incorporates these factors through the application of the Shapley value concept from game theory. Our approach ensures that users adhere to the specified consumption targets while maximizing individual profits. Our results demonstrate the existence and efficiency of the proposed ASDM solution, which can be effectively implemented within a competitive market environment. Numerical simulations showcase the advantages of this ASDM approach, particularly in comparison to non-cooperative and uniformly random strategies.

In order to investigate the link between black hole physics and the cosmological theory of Rastall, we have examined the influence of gravity on Hawking radiation in a more comprehensive Rastall framework. We have first determined the more accurate metric solutions for charged black string equations in this framework, taking into account the relationships between gravity, charge, and non-gravitational energy flux. These solutions have allowed us to calculate the more accurate temperature and energy emission rate for quantum black holes, and have shown that the Rastall theory modifies the non-rotating, spherically-symmetric black hole properties in a manner similar to the anti-de Sitter model. We have also found that the more accurate temperature and energy emission rate for quantum black holes are reduced compared to the general relativity, and have further explored the relationship between the speed of light and non-gravitational energy flux using the Rastall theory.

The results demonstrate that the power spectra of almost periodic functions and spectral measures associated with weakly mixing transformations have significant connections to the rates of convergence in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem. This reveals that for transformations with discrete spectra, specifically those exhibiting power spectrum bounds $[c_0, c_1]$ and spectral density $f$, the convergence rates are tied to the infimum of the slopes of the lines passing through $(c_0, f(c_0))$ and $(c_1, f(c_1))$. This relationship is further extended to transformations with infinite spectra, characterized by a lower spectral bound $c_0$ and an upper spectral bound $c_1$, provided that the power spectra exhibit convexity in this interval.

Identifying metal-poor star candidates using the Gaia space mission's photometric survey is crucial for discovering extremely ancient, halo stars. Although the mission's survey provides a vast amount of data, it lacks the resolution to distinguish the detailed spectral features necessary for determining a star's metal content using traditional methods. However, recent research has revealed that patterns within the mission's data can indicate a star's metal content. This study further develops this concept by analyzing how these patterns change when a star's metal content varies. It then uses machine learning to identify key features within the mission's data that are most indicative of metal content and develops a method to automatically classify stars based on this information. The researchers tested this method using simulated data and found that it was effective in determining a star's metal content with a high degree of accuracy. They then applied the method to real data from the mission's survey, which allowed them to identify metal-poor stars and discover potential candidates for extremely ancient, halo stars.

This research introduces the Global Fire Season Severity Index (GFSSI), an index designed to assess the severity of global fires. It utilizes a dataset of daily fire reports from the Fire Information for Resource Management system and a dataset of land cover information from the Global Land Cover Classification System. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of the GFSSI through various analyses, including examination of historical trends, correlation with climate patterns, and forecasting of fire severity. The results indicate that the GFSSI is a reliable tool, showing strong correlations with climate patterns and accurate predictions of fire severity. The research also identifies climate patterns as a key factor influencing fire severity. The authors employ a technique called transfer learning to develop a model that predicts fire severity based on climate pattern forecasts. The research demonstrates the potential of the GFSSI to support decision-making in fire management and highlights its limitations and areas for further study.

This study compares three distinct methods for evaluating the morphological complexity of languages. The first approach involves quantifying the morphological features present in a language's writing system. The second method assesses complexity based on a language's inherent characteristics, as determined by analysis of its corpora. The third approach relies on a time-based measure, accounting for factors like writing and speaking habits, as well as other factors like word order. We conducted a comprehensive examination of 41 languages, considering multiple factors, including a new corpus-based measure, a standardized frequency measure, speaker reports, and other metrics. We discovered that the three methods yield three distinct representations of complexity and that the morpheme-per-word frequency measure is the only one closely aligned with the corpus-based assessment. The study's findings suggest that the multiple complexity representations reflect different aspects of language and that the use of a single complexity measure may be inadequate.

Researchers have proposed self-interacting dark matter as a potential model for galaxy evolution within clusters, suggesting that dark matter may not be as uniform as previously thought.  To explore this idea, a recent study used gravitational lensing data from 10 galaxy clusters to test the possibility of self-interacting dark matter.  By analyzing the shear profiles of the clusters, the study found no evidence to support self-interaction, even at the smallest scales.  Furthermore, the results indicate that mass in these clusters primarily comes from dark matter, with visible matter contributing relatively little.  The study's findings have significant implications for our understanding of galaxy evolution within clusters, with the results most consistent with models where dark matter is nearly unperturbed by self-interaction.

This study focuses on reducing the complexity of parametric partial differential equations (PPDEs) by finding an accurate approximation space for the solution. Given incomplete information, we utilize a combination of available data and theoretical constraints to establish an accurate approximation space. Building on the theoretical framework of orthogonal projection, our approach involves iterative updates based on newly acquired information. This methodology can be applied to various types of PPDEs and our analysis shows that it results in an approximation space that closely matches the true solution space of the PPDE. Furthermore, our approach allows for the inclusion of theoretical errors in the approximation, enabling the controlled maintenance of theoretical accuracy errors. This methodology can be applied to various types of PPDEs and our analysis shows that it results in an approximation space that closely matches the true solution space of the PPDE.

This research presents a novel adaptation of the Independent Component Analysis Fast (ICAF) algorithm, tailored to address correlations in data subsets. By leveraging this modification, ICAF can analyze larger datasets within the same computational time as ICA. Our investigation into the causes of data subset inter-correlation led to the development of two new methods: identifying the most correlated subset or subspaces with minimal correlation. These methods were then applied to preprocessed data subsets before Independent Component Analysis computation. Our analysis revealed that ICAF applied to these subsets yields better results, specifically in terms of Performance Index, compared to the original algorithm.

Identifying significant social media events in real-time is crucial for understanding current situations and responding accordingly. Not only do breaking news stories change rapidly in terms of both location and time, but extracting meaningful events from the vast amounts of data shared on social media platforms like Twitter and Facebook presents a significant challenge due to the noise and redundancy inherent in user-generated content. Our proposed system effectively detects social media events in real-time by filtering out irrelevant data and identifying relevant locations and their associated event times using advanced natural language processing techniques and spatial analysis. The system incorporates a novel approach to separating events based on location and time, allowing it to accurately detect spatial and temporal patterns in data. The system's performance was validated through a series of experiments using actual social media data related to several significant events, and the results demonstrate its ability to accurately identify relevant events and discard irrelevant information.

We explore the existence, uniqueness, and stability of solutions to a certain type of elliptic equation that incorporates surface measures. Our study is grounded in a PDE reformulation of the Pansu-Lin equation, originally devised to describe isometric embeddings of surfaces in $\mathbb R^2$. By establishing a connection between the elliptic equation and the standard $H^2$-Neumann problem, we demonstrate the existence and stability of solutions. Our approach yields new insights into the Pansu-Lin equation, particularly regarding its singularity properties and the type of solution that can be achieved.

Advanced permanent magnets made from rare earth and transition metal alloys have been widely used for decades in various applications. To create cobalt-rich compounds that could serve as superior magnet materials, researchers have conducted an extensive search within the yttrium-cobalt-boron system using multiple potential candidates derived from crystal structure predictions and phase diagram analysis. Through simulations, two novel cobalt-rich phases were discovered: YCo$_{16}$ and YCo$_{20}$. These phases were found to exist under conditions similar to those found at earth's core temperature and pressure. Structural studies revealed that YCo$_{16}$ crystallizes in a C2/c space group with a tetragonal crystal structure, and further investigations using first-principles calculations confirmed its stability up to extremely high temperatures, ranging from 1800K to 3000K.

In the field of display advertising, real-time bidding has been the norm since its introduction in 2009. To optimize bidding strategies, researchers have developed various models that utilize auction house features and advertiser goals. This paper presents an adaptive bidding framework that adjusts for click fraud and takes into account a publisher's risk threshold and an advertiser's budget. The proposed strategy, based on an epsilon-first and epsilon-greedy algorithm, determines the optimal time to switch between types of bids as the auction progresses. The efficacy of this framework is demonstrated through simulations using actual traffic data from an online publisher and realistic advertiser scenarios.

Nonclassical properties in continuous-variable quantum systems are often marked by quantum correlations as well as the appearance of negative probabilities in phase space. Two key indicators, quantum steering and Wigner negativity, enable the assessment of nonclassical traits in these systems. Our investigation centers on the relationship between these two indicators, specifically how the presence of quantum steering influences the development of Wigner negativity in certain modes of an optical cavity field. We demonstrate that initial quantum steering can expedite the creation of Wigner negativity, particularly when combined with thermally disturbed cavity fields. Conversely, our study also examines how the initial disturbance of cavity fields can facilitate the steering of the state, revealing a reciprocal relationship between these two nonclassical traits.

Accurate secure boundary analysis is crucial for practical quantum key distribution systems, but the current method of analyzing secure boundaries assumes a uniformly distributed random seed, which does not fully account for potential non-uniformities during the generation process. To address this limitation, we have developed a new approach to analyze secure boundaries that takes into consideration the actual distribution of random seeds. This approach has been applied to two common quantum key distribution protocols, BB84 and decoy state, and we have found that the classical distance between Eve's states and the orthogonal base can be a suitable metric to analyze secure boundaries in general quantum key distribution systems, regardless of the distribution of random seeds.

This research paper confirms a long-standing conjecture by Ghosh and Santhanam by showing that certain types of curves do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves for all possible dimensions greater than one. We derive the necessary and sufficient conditions under which a class of curves would fit the classification, and further provide explicit equations to determine whether a curve fits the classification in terms of its direction field and the shape operator.

We investigate the diffusion process $X_t = t^{\beta} x_{\sqrt{t}}$ where $0 < \beta < 1$ and $x$ follows the Feller diffusion $dx = \sigma^2 dx - 2x dx + (2 \mu x + \sigma^2) dw_t$. Our work extends the results of Birkner and Matese (2016) to include a broader range of $\beta$ values, and we also analyze the asymptotic properties of the sampling distribution for the standardized sample means of these diffusion processes as the sample size becomes infinitely large.

In this work, we explore the scattering of complex light states within a coupled waveguide QED system, focusing on the interactions between multiple photons in the system. The scattering of multi-photon states, particularly those with high photon counts, is crucial for understanding the behavior of non-classical electromagnetic fields in confined environments. To investigate this phenomenon, we have developed a comprehensive theoretical framework based on a diagrammatic approach, which is rooted in a first-principles boson-integration formalism. This framework is capable of addressing a broad range of scattering problems, including multi-photon states, by leveraging a system of interacting bosons that represents the cavity and waveguide systems. Building upon this framework, we have derived a set of rules governing the diagrammatic expansion, which can be used to compute scattering amplitudes for complex light states. We have also demonstrated the efficacy of our framework by comparing our results for the scattering of two photons with existing analytical solutions, and we have further demonstrated the utility of our framework by examining the scattering of three-photon states. Our findings reveal that the behavior of three-photon states can exhibit non-analogous behavior when compared to classical electromagnetic fields, and we have also identified key signatures that can be used to distinguish between three-photon states and other types of states.

A potential way to study low-mass dark matter using direct detection experiments could be by examining the effects of spin-dependent interactions. This method has the advantage of being less susceptible to background interference compared to other approaches. In this paper, we explore the possibility of using high-energy dark matter particles produced in extremely powerful cosmic events and captured by massive objects such as the sun. These particles can interact with protons through a complex energy exchange, and our analysis reveals that a more sensitive detector configuration could be needed to achieve significant results.
This note employs Faulhaber's Formula to elucidate why odd Bernoulli numbers equate to zero.

Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shifts. Its operation can be broken down into two main stages: a conventional differential detection process followed by a delay-based detection method. The secondary step is critical in determining the overall system's bit error rate performance. This research investigates the optimal time discrepancy for various modulation formats like GMSK, Gaussian-shaped double-side pulse (GDBP), and raised cosine pulse (RC). Our findings indicate that an optimal time discrepancy exists for each modulation type and that its magnitude is directly related to the modulation's spectral characteristics. The secondary step has a significant influence on the overall system's spectral efficiency. This research presents the optimal time discrepancy for each modulation format and highlights its practical implications.

Reward learning is a crucial task in reinforcement learning where determining the optimal reward for each action state combination is a significant challenge. Most current methods rely on trial and error, but this is impractical due to the complexity of such combinations. In our research, we propose a visually-assisted approach to group similar action state combinations and leverage expert knowledge to identify their characteristics. By analyzing these groups, we can refine the reward function to improve the efficiency of reinforcement learning. The experimental results show that our method outperforms alternative techniques in reward learning.

Within the context of noncommutative space-time, we have revisited the electroweak structure functions of the nucleon, building on the massless fermion propagator analysis previously conducted. Our work has involved deriving the complete nucleon structure function sum rules, including those related to flavor, using noncommutativity-based gauge boson propagators, and has utilized the Operator Neutrino Deep Inelastic Scattering formalism to compute individual structure functions. Our findings, based on perturbative noncommutativity, reveal that even at high Bjorken-x, the nucleon's parton densities remain dominated by the quark contribution.

In topological quantum codes, a topological entanglement spectrum is expected to provide extensive information on the quantum phases of a system. Contrary to this notion, we have discovered that the entanglement spectrum of a frustrated Toric code model exhibits a one-dimensional topological structure, defying the Holographic Principle by creating a closed topological boundary within a two-dimensional system. This unique property arises due to the emergence of a single, interacting Majorana fermion mode, resulting from the system's non-trivial ground state. Furthermore, the mode can be represented as a single, topologically-protected edge mode, whose non-interacting counterpart is a Majorana fermion. The edge mode's interaction with itself is mediated by a non-local connection, exemplifying a form of 'glueing' in a topological context. Theoretical predictions have been substantiated through extensive numerical simulations.

We investigate the eigenspectra of large, randomly constructed Hermitian block matrices, whose structure is perturbed by a finite rank complex modification. Given that the band's width expands faster than the square root of the matrix's size, our analysis demonstrates that the statistical distribution of the imaginary components of the eigenvectors aligns with the results from the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble. This finding was achieved using the methods and approaches developed for models without complex modification.

Recent advancements in dialogue tasks have been achieved through pre-trained language models. However, current dialogue pre-training methods focus primarily on capturing the semantic meaning of dialogue text, ignoring other crucial aspects of dialogue such as syntax and discourse. Furthermore, current methods are task-specific and fail to generalize to other dialogue tasks. In our study, we present a pre-trained language model, called the UDS-LM, that incorporates multiple dialogue understanding tasks through a unified framework. The UDS-LM model is enhanced by a novel architecture that separates the dialogue context into semantic, syntactic, and discourse components. The model's effectiveness is demonstrated on multiple downstream dialogue tasks, outperforming strong baselines and achieving state-of-the-art performance on one task.

To establish trust in machine learning models, it's crucial for users to comprehend their underlying algorithms. This understanding enables individuals to make informed decisions about using these models in critical applications. However, existing research on measuring interpretability is limited due to a lack of a precise definition and a standardized evaluation method. Furthermore, existing metrics are often algorithm-specific and focus on measuring model outputs rather than the human understanding required to achieve those results. This research proposes a groundbreaking framework for measuring interpretability by incorporating essential cognitive skills that humans must acquire to learn an algorithm. This framework assesses three fundamental aspects: learning required marginal payoff, learning conditional relationships, and learning variable dependencies. Based on these components, a new interpretability metric is developed and tested using both human subject experiments and a widely used computer-based evaluation tool. The results demonstrate that this novel framework effectively captures the essence of human learning and outperforms existing algorithms in a real-world human subject study.

Anomaly detection using Isolation Forests has proven effective across various domains, thanks to their unique ability to excels in outlier detection and their simplicity in implementation. However, the original Isolation Forest algorithm has limitations that don't allow it to work in restricted environments such as low-resource devices and scenarios with limited labels. To address these issues, we've developed an enhanced version of the algorithm, leveraging the advantages of TinyML. By integrating a regularization technique based on regularization by hyperlane, we've successfully adapted the isolation algorithm to work with sparse labels. Our approach has been thoroughly tested and validated in scenarios with resource constraints, yielding impressive results that outperform the baseline methods in anomaly detection.

A common statistical model used to model extreme events uses a transformed variable with a specific distribution, often assuming a normal or lognormal transformation results in a variable that follows an extreme-value distribution. However, this approach can lead to inaccurate inferences when observing a subset of all events, as it fails to account for non-extreme values. A new method addresses this issue by reparameterizing the extreme-value distribution to model the time between extreme events using a Poisson process. This reparameterized model has the advantage of providing accurate inferences for extreme events, while also enabling comparisons of joint extreme event probabilities. The method's performance is demonstrated through a Bayesian inference simulation, showcasing its applications in various real-life scenarios such as comparing droughts and floods.

This study examines the average cross-section in a particular region where the average speed remains stationary, using a method adapted from probability theory and the method of characteristics. A formula is derived to calculate the speed distribution $\sigma(\eta,\xi)$ based on a single parameter $\eta$. It is found that the speed distribution is determined by a single variable $\xi$, which can take on values between 0 and $\eta$. The average cross-section is found to be stationary when the speed function is uniformly distributed. Several models are presented to illustrate these findings.

Developing a knowledge graph that comprehensively captures everyday, informal knowledge has been a long-standing challenge in the field of natural language processing. The COMET knowledge graph, created through a massive language dataset, provides a wealth of everyday knowledge, covering 12 distinct categories of human behavior and emotional responses. A companion dataset, ATOMIC, symbolically represents the causal relationships between these knowledge categories. The continued growth of the COMET graph and associated datasets holds significant potential for significant advancements in future AI research.

We introduce the data processing pipeline developed for the Hi-GAL survey, a key component of the Herschel SPIRE Project.
This pipeline leverages the HECA reduction pipeline to produce Hi-GAL data products, specifically 20, 50, 100, 200, and 400 map sets in various frequency bands.
Our pipeline further includes additional steps to produce 350 $\mu$m maps, apply photometric calibration, and calculate key physical and spectral energy distribution parameters for thousands of dense molecular cloud cores.
Ultimately, the full release of Hi-GAL data products will comprise over 2 Tbit of comprehensive data spanning 21 frequency bands, 67 square degrees, and three SPIRE data products, available through the Herschel Science Archive.

Recent studies of the globular cluster NGC 2808 using photometric techniques suggested the presence of multiple stellar populations with distinct metal content. To verify these findings, we employed high-resolution spectroscopy to measure the iron abundance of 55 bright red giant stars in the cluster. Our analysis used spectra with a resolution of 60,000 collected as part of the ESPaDOnS program at the VLT. We calculated the iron abundance for each star using standard methods and considered potential errors. Our results revealed a mean iron abundance of -1.51 ± 0.04 and a standard deviation of 0.10, indicating a spread in iron levels among the stars. Our analysis also showed a correlation between iron abundance and temperature, but no correlation with star brightness. Our findings supported the earlier photometric results, confirming the presence of multiple stellar populations in NGC 2808.

To gain insights into the behavior of active particles, particularly in crowded conditions, we utilize the concept of single file diffusion to study the entropic forces acting on exiting particles. By employing the first exit time from a semi-infinite one-dimensional confining space, we investigate the speed-accuracy relationship of exit times. The speed is gauged by the mean exit time, while accuracy is evaluated by the time variability. The mean exit time exhibits a notable decrease as the particle's speed increases, accompanied by increasing disorder (variance) at higher speeds. Notably, the time variability displays a non-monotonic trend, rising with moderate speeds before stabilizing at higher speeds. These findings are supported by analytical calculations and simulations, offering valuable insights into the behavior of active particles in crowded environments.

Quantum Mechanics challenges the long-held assumption that inferences based on previous observations must be consistent. Our research reveals that quantum-level inferences do indeed follow a consistent pattern, which is actually a natural extension of Bayes' rule. Moreover, we show that any smaller system isomorphic to a qubit must have its inferences consistent in both cases. Interestingly, the incoherent blending of information, which is used when quantum-level data is mixed, does not affect its inherent consistency. Our results also indicate that the incoherent blending of information does not contradict the consistency of inferences. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the incoherent blending of information is a natural consequence of the fact that inferences based on different observations are themselves mutually exclusive.

We examine whether the QCD equation of state differs in small interaction volumes relative to its large-system counterpart. We investigate this question using the lattice QCD perturbative theory as of early 2021, applying various lattice volumes and proxy indicators, such as hadron gas degeneracies and internal momenta distributions. Our findings suggest that the pressure of quark-gluon plasma and SU(N) pure gauge liquid, when normalized by their respective entropy densities, behave identically in small volumes relative to their large-system counterparts. However, the ratio of energy to entropy density in the quark-gluon plasma displays a noticeable deviation from its large-system value, particularly at low temperatures and various latice volumes. Additionally, the internal energy contributions of quarks and gluons in the quark-gluon plasma show significant deviations from their respective hadron gas limits.

Let's consider the graded algebra generated by the Steenrod algebra with its natural action on the integers modulo 2. We can extend the integers modulo 2 to a suitable total space for a Milnor basis of the algebra, and this allows us to identify that the algebra's cohomology with coefficients in integers modulo 2 is isomorphic to a specific linear combination of the algebra itself and a specific linear combination of integers modulo 2, where the formula for the combination depends on the total space's topological structure, which is topologically equivalent to a sphere of a specific dimension.

Space-based telescopes have been observing the Lyman ultraviolet region of the electromagnetic spectrum since the launch of the Hubble Space Telescope in 1990, a span of nearly three decades. Despite this, photometric accuracy in UV astronomy has been hindered by the presence of Lyman-alpha forest emissions, a type of quasilinear absorption feature that affects wavelength ranges between 1210 and 1218 angstroms. Researchers have proposed the Lyman-alpha Filter Prototype, an innovative device capable of reducing the sensitivity of UV spectrographs to wavelengths outside of its 1207-1210 angstrom range while highly responsive within the 1210-1218 angstrom band. The instrument would be integrated into a space-based UV spectrograph to enable photometric accuracy in regions with Ly-alpha forest emissions. The Ly-alpha Filter Prototype is an innovative device that utilizes a modulated absorption feature to selectively amplify a specific frequency of light. The device achieves its selectivity through the precise adjustment of its center frequency, spanning a range of 115-135 nanometers. The Ly-alpha Filter Prototype's effectiveness was tested using a simulated UV spectrum containing various types of absorption features. The results showed that the device produced a high signal-to-noise ratio of 100:1 while maintaining a 3% precision in its center frequency adjustment. The device's accuracy was further validated by comparing its performance with a reference standard. The researchers also explored the potential applications of the Ly-alpha Filter Prototype in enabling photometric accuracy in

Optimal distributed control systems for graph-based systems can be interpreted as a coordinated action among distinct entities to achieve a shared goal. Graph filter technology has revolutionized the processing of graph-based signals, drawing inspiration from FFT and filter design concepts. Building upon this foundation, our research focuses on developing innovative solutions for optimal distributed control systems. Specifically, we introduce a novel class of optimal controllers, referred to as G2 controllers, which leverage graph signal processing principles to achieve a dual objective: minimizing communication overhead and capturing the essence of graph connectivity through positive semi-definite matrices. Our theoretical framework demonstrates that G2 controllers are inherently optimal for specific graph configurations and provide a distributed means of achieving this optimality. Moreover, our research showcases the practical efficacy of G2 controllers by comparing them to traditional methods in numerical experiments.

Image search algorithms often struggle due to image retrieval task limitations, such as processing variations in image representations, accounting for diverse user queries, and adapting to new data distributions. To address these challenges, we propose the active image indexing method, which proactively seeks optimal boundaries between regions of the feature space. Our approach is based on a hierarchical clustering technique that employs a Gaussian mixture model to facilitate efficient retrieval and representation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in tackling the inherent difficulties in the image representation problem through empirical analysis and experiments. Additionally, we develop and release the Active Image Indexing library to enable researchers in the visual search community to build more robust and efficient image representations.

This study introduces an innovative concept for authentication in channel scenarios where transmission loss patterns are unpredictable. Building upon a novel framework, a channel encoder is combined with an authenticator in an integrated system. Messages are divided into segments, encrypted, and sent over the channel in sequential order. Receivers verify authenticity by comparing the order in which they receive the segments with the intended order intended by the sender. This concept's feasibility and performance are evaluated in terms of maximum error probability and maximum secure key rate. Optimal channel encoding schemes are identified, and their specific implementations are determined. Numerical results demonstrate that our solution can efficiently secure communication even when there's no key exchange, and the order of the encoded data matters to prevent unauthorized access.

We investigate the phase diagram of classical over-damped particles in a washboard potential, focusing on the transition from localized to delocalized states. Our analysis reveals that this transition can be accurately described using a disorder-averaged one-dimensional equation. We confirm this by comparing it to a more complex, higher-dimensional Liouville equation. The resulting phase diagram consists of two distinct regions separated by a boundary along which the equation simplifies to the Langevin equation. For localized states below this boundary, our equation accurately predicts the spatial distribution of the particles' return times. Conversely, for delocalized states above this boundary, these return times become randomly distributed. We further demonstrate that this equation effectively describes the emergence of dispersionless states, a phenomenon predicted by a simplified, integrable model.

This paper presents an adaptable, localized predictive technique that builds upon Jord\'a's (2005) model, expanding it to a semi-parametric multi-stage approach. Initially, the study employs negative binomial regression to estimate event likelihood, then explores the impact of events on a variable via a non-parametric analysis and finally constructs a predictive model, utilizing a Generalized Linear Model's response function, to forecast changes in event-related variables. A simulation revealed that the novel approach results in more accurate predictions compared to the traditional method. To demonstrate its practicality, the estimated predictive equations were constructed for five scenarios: the effect of financial crises on inflation, recession duration, stock market volatility, commodity price fluctuations, and SARS recovery rates.

We investigate the influence of the electromagnetic quantum vacuum on a charge $q$, which orbits at a distance $r$ away from a strong magnetic field. The angular momentum generated by the vacuum effects can be computed using two methods: first, by examining the non-relativistic electromagnetic field's one-loop effective action; and second, by deriving the angular momentum of a rigid charge on a wire, which has been studied in the past, and then applying classical thermodynamics to obtain the effective action and angular momentum of a free charge. Our results demonstrate that the effective action and angular momentum of a free charge differ from those of a charge on a wire. We calculate the specific angular momentum contribution from the vacuum effects for a charge in the $n$-th Landau level and find that it scales as $q^2r^2\alpha^2_{\text{QED}} n^2$. For comparison, we also compute the specific angular momentum of a free charge in the $n$-th Landau level using the Dirac propagator and find that it scales as $q^2r^2\alpha^2_{\text{QED}} n^4$.

A crucial yet complex task known as fine-grained named entity typing (FGET) demands precise identification of entity subtypes from a limited set of options. Many existing models struggle to perform well due to the issue of label scarcity, where there are too many potential labels and not enough instances. To address this challenge, we propose FGNET-RH, a pioneering approach that uses a combination of hyperbolic embedding and hierarchical refinement to effectively tackle FGET. By incorporating a hierarchical framework with parent-child relationships, FGNET-RH is able to capture long-term contextual dependencies and improve its performance. The model's refinement mechanism in hyperbolic space allows it to iteratively refine entity representations and make more accurate predictions. The parent node's refined representation serves as a better proxy for its child entities, leading to improved performance. The model's effectiveness was evaluated on four benchmark datasets, demonstrating significant gains over existing state-of-the-art models.

This paper establishes upper limits on the Hankel determinants for the $H_2(3)(f)$ and $H_2(4)(f)$ special types, considering a function $f$ within the univalent class $\mathcal{U}$. Furthermore, it provides optimal bounds for the special Hankel determinants $H_2(3)(\sigma)$ and $H_2(4)(\sigma)$, with the function $\sigma$ belonging to the $\mathcal{U}$ class and being expressed using the Janowski variables. Additionally, it derives general bounds for the special Hankel determinants $H_2(3)(\phi)$ and $H_2(4)(\phi)$, with the function $\phi$ adhering to the $\mathcal{U}$ class and being defined by the Koebe-$(0, 1)$ extremal function.

Achieving efficient load balancing in a data center is crucial to prevent overutilization and ensure timely response to urgent cloud requests. This research proposes an innovative placement strategy that anticipates future resource demands and prevents hotspots. The proposed method, Prepartition, utilizes predictive models and real-time data to distribute workload ahead of time. Prepartition adjusts the scheduling policy in a manner similar to partition load balancing. The proposed approach was evaluated using a real dataset and compared to current techniques. Results demonstrate that Prepartition outperforms existing methods, including MaxMin, which can lead to a 40% reduction in response time for high-priority requests and 20% for low-priority requests, while also preventing overutilization and ensuring timely responses to urgent cloud requests.

We introduce Fixed Point Networks (FPNs), a class of neural networks capable of modeling dynamical systems that reach equilibrium through the use of fixed point methods. By training an FPN on time-series data, it learns a mapping where initial conditions are connected to their corresponding equilibrium points. FPNs offer several benefits, including the ability to directly predict system equilibrium, even when it's not reachable via typical methods, and avoiding unstable trajectories that can't be captured by traditional models. In this work, we explore the theoretical framework for FPNs and demonstrate their effectiveness in modeling various systems through both theoretical analysis and practical applications.

This study aims to determine bounding limits for the causal effects in experiments, using a concept within a framework that assumes no unmeasured confounding variables. The main advantage of the proposed method is its ability to calculate bounds for the causal effects in experiments without requiring an empirical version of the causal model being identifiable. The method is particularly useful in high-dimensional settings where traditional methods fail due to issues of dimensionality and dependence. The performance of the new approach is demonstrated through its application to simulated data and actual clinical trials, involving cancer patients' expression profiles.

This research focuses on developing an early alert system that can identify and notify users of an impending attack on LTI systems that uses limited real-time data. The proposed warning system utilizes an unsupervised anomaly detection method incorporating a statistical test to identify unexpected system behavior indicated by significant deviations from expected trends. By leveraging spectral limitations, the attack detection time is optimized. The proposed warning system effectively addresses stealthy cyber attacks that aim to evade detection by maintaining a normal system appearance. The method's performance is demonstrated through successful predictions of several attack scenarios, outperforming a baseline model that relies on a simple moving average for comparison.

A precise summary can be derived from lengthy written documents via deep learning models, but English language models often benefit from larger training sets and pre-trained tools, whereas summarization for lesser-known Indian languages is hindered by complex syntax and differences in meaning. Our research proposes GAE-ISumm, a method that uses a unique graph structure to translate these complexities, starting with sentence sets that are then ranked and selected using a unique algorithm to create summaries. Our experiments demonstrate that GAE-ISumm consistently produces high-quality summaries that are verified by human readers, outperforming alternative methods across various evaluations.

We establish the definition and certain attributes of S-rings of Krull type, in addition to examining the relationship between the dimension of an S-ring of type A in one dimension and that of its dimension's extension. We also calculate the dimension of the extension's dimension. Furthermore, an example is given of an S-ring that is equal to the union of its sub-S-rings but does not satisfy the condition of being an upper semi-lattice structure. In addition, an example is provided of an S-ring that is not sequentially orderable but has an extension that is sequentially orderable.

Researchers have identified five stars that have accelerated in their movement across the sky over the past few decades. This observation was made using data from the Hipparcos satellite. Four out of the five stars appear to be moving in random directions, suggesting their motion is due to gravitational influence. Their mass is estimated to be in the range of 0.5 to 2.5 solar masses. Their acceleration can be explained if a companion with a mass of at least 0.3 to 1.2 solar masses exists within a certain distance from each other, typically under 1000 thousand kilometers. The only exception is for the star, HD 24040, where its acceleration can be explained if a companion with a mass of at least 3.5 solar masses exists within a certain distance from the star, typically under 100 thousand kilometers. We introduce the least square variational Bayesian Autoencoder, a novel generative model that generates realistic natural image data. By utilizing the least square variational Bayesian Autoencoder, we are able to derive a precise variational posterior from the approximate distribution of the latent variables, without relying on stochastic gradient descent for optimization. The performance of the model is evaluated through various metrics and qualitative assessments, demonstrating its ability to produce high-quality natural image samples and achieve precise variational posterior approximations. Notably, the findings suggest that the least square variational Bayesian Autoencoder outperforms the traditional variational Bayesian Autoencoder, particularly in terms of posterior precision and image quality.

Smart home technology has seen significant growth due to increasing accessibility and cost reductions, driven by the proliferation of low-cost, highly capable sensors and devices. However, this trend also raises serious security and reliability concerns, particularly in relation to maintaining residents' privacy and well-being. This study proposes an integrated framework for monitoring smart home devices, combining private blockchain technology with location-based tracking. Our approach employs a private blockchain to verify sensor data authenticity, while a location-based system ensures that unauthorized access is blocked. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework in addressing the primary challenges facing smart home technology.

A novel approach to quantizing log-likelihood ratio storage utilizes deep learning, where a fully connected neural network maps input L-values to compressed binary codes. This scheme, termed deep quantization, achieves superior performance by generating accurate L-value representations. Our findings demonstrate that employing a neural network to combine local L-value features leads to enhanced performance compared to conventional approaches. Notably, the deep quantization scheme outperforms one of the best known methods, Tied-Component MMSE, in terms of error rate. However, it does so at the cost of increased computational complexity.

However, this particular question proves to be challenging under a fixed-parameter approach, given the involved parameters. Our research shows that the following issues are, in fact, fixed-parameter tractable: the parameterized FPT algorithms for the upward planarity also solve the problem of checking if a graph can be turned into a planar layout with specific constraints. Crowdsourced data is frequently utilized to gather labels for images, which are then employed in various machine learning applications, such as object detection and classification. However, the reliability of these labels is compromised due to the inaccuracies introduced during the data collection process. These errors can be attributed to several factors, such as misinterpretation of the task instructions or random mistakes. In this research, we investigate the application of Bayesian ensemble modeling to overcome label noise. To quantify the uncertainty associated with each label, we develop a method that estimates the entropy of the crowd's response distribution. We demonstrate that incorporating this uncertainty into the training process can effectively mitigate the negative impact of noisy labels. We evaluate our approach on the ImageNet dataset using state-of-the-art convolutional neural network architectures, which includes a model architecture inspired by ResNet-50.

For semiflows with uniformly or nonuniformly expanding dynamics, which exhibit exponential decay in correlations, we prove the exponential decay in the H\"older norm of the transfer operators acting on smooth observables.

A particular matrix known as a covering array has specific properties. It must have rows and columns with distinct symbols from a limited set, and it satisfies a condition known as cover property. The array's size is measured by the number of rows and it has a minimum size defined by a formula based on the number of columns and the number of each column's unique symbols. A particular type of matrix known as a strength-2 covering array has additional properties. It satisfies a stronger version of the cover property and it has a limited number of certain patterns in its columns. In this study, we examined the structure of small size-2 covering arrays. By analyzing them based on different patterns and their occurrences, we identified some key characteristics. We used this information to find all size-2 covering arrays for 12 different situations and we found general formulas for some of them. The arrays found in this study are available online.

Research demonstrates that players with access to a noisy channel can produce a nearly maximally entangled state with certainty, where the degree of noise is quantifiable by a real value between 0 and 1. We establish that when two players employ a strategy involving a nonlocal game using orthonormal operators, their ability to produce this near-maximally entangled state is directly linked to the game's decidability. Specifically, if a nonlocal game can be solved perfectly, it follows that for any level of noise less than 1, players using that level of noisy maximally entangled state will win the game with certainty. Conversely, if a nonlocal game cannot be solved perfectly, it is possible that players using noisy maximally entangled states at any level of noise can win the game with certainty.

This study partially replicates the work by Soltani et al. who developed a genetic algorithm to systematically trigger Java stacktrace errors. The original study demonstrated the algorithm's effectiveness in reproducing crashes on a test dataset, but this paper focuses on replicating the results to evaluate the algorithm's reliability. By applying the algorithm to multiple engineers' fault symbols, we found that it successfully triggered the desired errors and, in addition, uncovered new failure patterns not previously documented. Notably, the algorithm's convergence issues and sensitivity to hyperparameter adjustments were also observed, which may impact its generalizability to other domains.

The vortex lattice in superconductors undergoes various phase transitions as the magnetic field is altered. Researchers have investigated these transitions in the strongly anisotropic high-Tc cuprate superconductor YBa2Cu3O6.58 over a wide temperature range. As the magnetic field is rotated relative to the crystallographic axes, distinct square-to-quadrupole transition shifts were observed, consistent with both pinning and fluxonic mechanisms. Furthermore, the observed square vortex lattice pattern persisted at temperatures as low as 4 K. In contrast, the vortex lattice was undetectable below 4 K in the same material when the magnetic field was aligned with the crystallographic axes, suggesting the presence of flux creep due to strong disorder.

The elliptic anisotropic flow of thermal photons in relativistic heavy-ion collisions is investigated using a transport model that simulates these collisions. It's discovered that the nuclear density and initial condition play a significant role in how photons move at the level of the fluid, which is influenced by the speed of light. The movement of photons is also affected by the properties of the medium it's moving through, specifically its viscosity and temperature. The study finds a correlation between the viscosity and movement of photons, which could be used to determine the properties of the medium. The study also finds that using photons from the most central collisions doesn't provide enough information to determine the properties of the medium due to the lack of data and high statistical uncertainty. The study suggests that using photons from less central, but still significant, collisions could provide more accurate information about the properties of the medium. The study also finds that using photons from specific angles could provide more accurate information about the properties of the initial condition, which could provide more insights into the early stages of the collisions.

A comprehensive study of regular magnetic orders on a triangular and kagome lattice is conducted using a classical Heisenberg model. Multiple magnetic structures, including collinear, non-collinear, and ferri/ferro-magnetic types, are considered. The precise magnetic order parameters are formulated and the corresponding energy is derived. The energy expression's analytical properties are examined, particularly concerning its components and the wavenumber. Numerical calculations are performed to determine the phase diagram of the model. The findings reveal that certain magnetic structures can exhibit a larger number of phases compared to others, and that some of these phases may be stabilized through frustration effects. The study also identifies phase transitions that shift from first-order to continuous as the parameter values change. The results can serve as a foundation for investigating more complex magnetic structures and the corresponding phase transitions in triangular and kagome systems.

Large-scale online retailers employ numerous product promotions, resulting in a vast number of controlled experiments being conducted on various customer segments. Each experiment aims to determine the impact of a specific promotion by comparing the outcomes of treated and non-treated groups. Traditional statistical analysis methods often struggle with common real-world challenges such as non-normal data distributions, differing treatment effects across multiple metrics, and various types of customer segment divisions. To address these complexities, our approach develops an adaptive procedure that accurately detects treatment effects while maintaining an acceptable false discovery rate. This procedure leverages a weighted multi-arm procedure to maximize statistical power and control the false discovery rate through a heuristically-designed 'fair' weight function. By using a specific type of customer segmentation, our approach ensures that our method remains valid even in the presence of strong dependencies within the data.

The foundational aspects of cosmological inflation are addressed. The derivation of equations governing the inflaton field, an introduction to slow-roll parameters, and a description of how inflationary perturbations correspond to cosmic microwave background temperature fluctuations are presented.

We investigate the Type-X two Higgs doublet model to see if it can resolve two major discrepancies in the Standard Model, specifically the muon's anomalous magnetic moment and the W boson's mass. Our analysis focuses on the type-X interaction, where muons primarily interact with a particular neutral Higgs boson through the SM s-channel. We calculate the total cross section for this interaction and use it to determine the effective coupling between the Higgs boson and the muon. Our results show that, given the current experimental constraints on the type-X interaction, it's challenging to satisfy both the muon's anomalous magnetic moment and W boson mass data simultaneously. However, it's possible to satisfy either the muon's anomalous magnetic moment or the W boson mass anomaly, depending on the type-X interaction parameters.

Software developers often face the challenge of searching for relevant information within software documentation, but many technical terms in these documents are poorly indexed due to their complex and nuanced meanings. As a result, developers need to adapt and refine search terms to get the desired results, a process that can be time-consuming and labor-intensive. To address this issue, we've developed a tool called QUICKAR, a query reformulation assistant that suggests alternative search terms to speed up concept location tasks. By leveraging crowdsourced data and natural language processing, QUICKAR identifies relevant synonyms and refines them based on their performance in actual concept location tasks, taking into account factors like precision and recall. In our experiments, QUICKAR consistently outperformed traditional search methods, suggesting it as a useful tool for software maintenance and development.

In interactions between people, the practice of adapting speech patterns to match another's characteristics is a fundamental aspect of establishing a connection. Entrainment, the reciprocal adaptation of speech characteristics, is a key indicator of social and emotional connections. Although previous studies have investigated entrainment in controlled settings, there is a lack of comprehensive research on how to accurately and reliably measure entrainment features in real-world conversations through speech patterns. This study aims to develop effective unsupervised methods for comparing entrainment using speech characteristics across various conditions. We begin by validating a novel feature set for measuring entrainment, then design two approaches based on autoencoders and recurrent neural networks to analyze this feature set. Our findings demonstrate the success of these methods in capturing distinct aspects of entrainment and provide a foundation for future research on entrainment in real-world conversations.

We've developed an open-source suite of web visualizers, called RCSEDv2, which enables researchers to easily display and analyze large datasets, including SEDs and images, utilizing JavaScript and Python. The package comprises three primary components: a spectral energy distribution visualizer derived from AstroPy's SedPlot, an image analysis tool derived from Astropy's display_utils, and a time-series visualizer specifically designed for transient data. Our tools are designed to be highly customizable, allowing users to select from a range of data sources, including VOTable, Astropy objects, and CSV files, and to customize the display with a variety of options, including colors, fonts, and grid configurations. In addition to facilitating data visualization, RCSEDv2 includes a simple web server for local hosting and a basic online demo. Our package is available for download under a flexible open-source license and can be accessed directly at rcsv2.net.

This paper introduces a novel, unsupervised method for identifying and categorizing specific actions within continuous video streams. A core challenge in understanding human activities lies in distinguishing between temporal sequences of events. To overcome the obstacle of insufficient annotated data, we propose an innovative, self-supervised approach to segment and analyze action sequences without the need for explicit category labels. A key aspect of our method involves generating contrastive features from aggregated video segments, which enables robust and high-level representations for temporal action identification. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed technique, yielding state-of-the-art performance on established benchmarks.

To identify possible $S$-wave hidden-charm pentaquark states, we have used the combination of quark and diquark, and then the quark-symmetric combination in the absence of diquarks as our two relevant bases. Through the application of current algebra, we have determined the properties of the two types of SU(3) representations, and subsequently, we have established the existence of three $S$-wave hidden-charm pentaquark states, specifically $\bar{X}(3010)$, $X(2900)$, and $\bar{X}(2900)$, and have determined their quantum numbers, and decay patterns. Our model also predicts the narrow resonances observed in experiments, and has identified the possible decay channels for these pentaquark states, including $\Sigma_c\bar{D}^{*}$, $\Sigma_c^{*}\bar{D}^{*}$, $\Xi_c\bar{D}^{*}$, and $\Xi_c'\bar{D}^{*}$.

The traditional approach to providing feedback in skill assessment often leads to overwhelming students with extensive comments, which can actually be counterproductive. To address this, we investigated the effectiveness of a more streamlined approach, where students receive general feedback at the general topic level, rather than detailed, specific criticism. We compared this approach to one that provided specific, detailed feedback and analyzed the resulting effects on students' performance in a specific context, an introductory software testing course. We examined student performance in terms of three key areas: learning outcomes, exam performance, and overall course grades. Our analysis revealed that students who received general feedback demonstrated improved exam results and increased course grades, while those who received detailed feedback showed no such advantages. These findings suggest that providing general feedback can be a more effective way to encourage students to learn and can help improve their performance in a learning environment.

Domain adaptation is a challenge when source domain data is inaccessible. A novel approach to address this issue proposed in this paper involves utilizing pseudo-label information from a related domain. A significant limitation of previous methods in this area is the requirement for significant user input. To overcome this, our framework decouples the hypothesis selection from the hypothesis training processes, allowing for the former to be performed on a fully supervised dataset. A related domain is then used to generate pseudo-labels for the selected hypothesis. Experimentation across multiple text-to-text tasks confirms the effectiveness of our method.

A novel type of nuclear reactor, the Gas Core Reactor, has the potential to significantly reduce travel times to distant celestial bodies in our solar system by leveraging nuclear propulsion technologies. This report provides a comprehensive overview of GCR physics and mathematics, covering the underlying principles, current research approaches, and recent numerical simulations. It includes an in-depth analysis of a specific GCR design, which utilizes an advanced fuel compound containing carbon nanotubes and requires extremely high temperatures to function effectively. The report also outlines the necessary steps for further investigation, including developing specialized computer software and conducting detailed numerical simulations of the reactor's behavior.

This paper presents a novel neural network architecture, the Domain-informed Neural Network, or DNet. DNet incorporates a layer that utilizes a domain-informed component to represent the neural network's output as a product of two functions - one that is inherently domain-informed and subjective to training, and another that is entirely learned by the network. Our research demonstrates that DNet's domain-informed component closely mirrors the network's performance, regardless of being trained jointly or independently. This finding suggests that DNet's domain-informed component effectively condenses complex information into the domain's parameters, much like human experts. Our study further shows that DNet's domain-informed component can be utilized to generate human-like explanations of the network's decision-making processes.

We introduce EXOPLINES, an open-access database of the specific absorption rates of molecular species found in the atmospheres of brown dwarfs and gas giants. The collection includes precise data on the specific absorption rates of 13 key molecules, covering an extensive temperature range (600-2000 K) and broad spectral coverage (0.36-50 $\mu$m). The specific absorption rates in EXOPLINES are calculated using accurate models of the molecules' behavior under various thermal conditions, superseding previous estimates that were often based on outdated models. We discuss the potential impact of these revised specific absorption rates on the study of substellar objects and giant exoplanets, highlighting the need for updated specific absorption rates records in line with the latest scientific understanding. The database can be accessed online at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7370510.

This text outlines the underlying principles of grounding processes in Answer Set Programming, providing a comprehensive semantic framework that encompasses existing methods as special cases. It distinguishes between operational methods generating a grounder, a processor, and a system, and identifies semantic aspects that must be preserved in the final grounding. The paper also examines how the final grounding's structure is affected by different operational methods. Furthermore, it investigates when partial grounding semantics apply and discusses an operational inconsistency based on well-founded models. The proposed framework is relevant to researchers working on various aspects of Answer Set Programming, including reasoning tasks, optimization, constraints, and learning.

We have established a fundamental principle for quantum information theories based on a set of fundamental resources. The law describes how a quantum state of the system and its surroundings change in time, with the temporal variation of the system's resource being dictated by the theory's constraints. The proof of this first law relies on the resource theory's inherent properties, including the ability to freely prepare states and the existence of an operational resource map. Our finding applies to a broad range of quantum information theories, encompassing scenarios like thermodynamics, causal influence, and quantum privacy, thus providing a unified framework for understanding these theories.

To represent information measures through random variable characteristics, we employ a higher-order statistical approach and derive higher-order approximations of the Kullback-Leibler divergence and Shannon entropy, using a maximum entropy principle. The resulting expressions show that lower-order approximations correspond to lower-order moment-based estimators for these information measures. The performance of these estimators is evaluated in a context of data analysis, where we discuss their advantages and limitations by means of numerical examples.

We analyze a single observation from a non-stationary, multivariate time series model characterized by heavy-tailed distributions and exhibit their statistical behavior. This model is particularly relevant in internet traffic analysis, a field where we investigate a unique observation, an internet hub's traffic flow. Our findings reveal that, in the high-traffic regime, the test statistic's distribution exhibits a non-standard, heavy-tailed asymptotic behavior, specifically belonging to the Poisson-Paradox class. Consequently, standard inferential methods are ineffective, and we develop and propose an alternative, more accurate estimator. Our analysis is supported by theoretical results and extensive numerical simulations, and we further validate our methods by applying them to real-world data from an internet service provider, demonstrating their practical utility in a business setting.

A novel set of quantum low-density parity-check codes is introduced, featuring explicit constructions and linear time decoders. The codes can be decoded in O(log n) rounds of parallel processing and possess a threshold similar to that of random quantum LDPC codes. The associated maximum likelihood decoder has a constant probability of error when applied to instances drawn from the standard symmetric quantum channel. The code's specifications, including its connectivity pattern and degree distribution, are explicitly stated, enabling straightforward implementation.

The distance-$r$ dominating set problem, a more complex variant of the dominating set problem, has been studied in approximation algorithms. For specific types of graphs with restricted expansion, such as those derived from lattices or certain regular lattices, previous solutions had achieved improved approximation ratios. In contrast, we have developed a different approach for a broader family of graphs with restricted expansion, applying a simple linear program to find a better approximation ratio of $(1-\frac{1}{t})\Delta + \frac{K_t-1}{\Delta}$. The performance of our algorithm heavily depends on the properties of the output of the linear program, and we have shown its applicability for specific values of $r$ and $t$.

In a theoretical study, researchers have examined the characteristics of bulk-boundary correspondence for high-order topological insulators in the presence of randomness. They demonstrated that even with edge disorder, high-order topological materials still exhibit protected higher-order boundaries, distinguished by unique properties. Specifically, surface states on higher-order boundaries of 3D TIs exhibit 2D topological characteristics opposite to those of 2D topological materials, in contrast to their 2D counterparts. This unique property allows the identification of protected boundaries from random bulk disorder. Furthermore, numerical simulations confirmed that disorder does not hinder the bulk-boundary correspondence in high-order TIs. This study contributes to understanding the relationship between bulk and boundary properties in high-order TIs under uncertainty.

This paper summarises various CMS searches for supersymmetry, focusing on extensive proton-proton collisions with a total energy of 139 inverse femtobarns recorded at 13 TeV. Diverse supersymmetry production modes are examined to determine the presence of various supersymmetry particles, including final-state signatures with multiple leptons, jets, b-tagged jets, transverse-energy maxima, Higgs bosons, missing energy, and long-lived particles. Supersymmetry scenarios are investigated under distinct theoretical models, and these results are interpreted in simplified models and specific theories like gauge-mediated supersymmetry with dark matter coannihilators.

Novel view synthesis with light field rendering traditionally achieves accurate reproduction of view-dependent phenomena by directly estimating every target view's radiance from reference views. However, this approach demands a substantial amount of reference data which can be difficult to obtain, especially when dealing with large and dynamic scenes. In contrast, light field neural rendering tackles view-dependent effects as a separate consideration, allowing it to generate reference views more efficiently with fewer resources. By doing so, it's feasible to acquire and store reference views more conveniently, ultimately leading to superior performance. Our method leverages the strengths of both perspectives and employs an alternative view representation that combines the benefits of epipolar and baropolar (view-angle-based) coherence, thereby facilitating more efficient neural rendering.

Observations from the IOTA system combining data from Hawaii and Arizona, yielded measurements for 13 targets. Additional interferometric observations using the PAQ, were successful for 8 unique systems, with some additional multi-aperture interferometry data collected through PACO, amounting to 10 new measurements. A total of 24 targets benefited from having their angular separations measured through speckle interferometry at the SOAR telescope.

We investigate chiral celestial sphere algebras linked to simple Lie algebras, their representations and cross-ratio domains. We establish that the chiral algebras formed this way possess a natural $W_1+\infty$ integrability characteristic of classical conformal systems. We also derive a corresponding BMS$_4$ symmetry from this property. Furthermore, we link the resulting chiral celestial algebras to colour-kinematics duality, demonstrating that they underlie the duality when applied to four-dimensional Yang-Mills theory. This work lays groundwork for applying the chiral model to four-dimensional gravity in the next stage.

A high-resolution radio observation of a solar flare on October 12, 2001, shows how type III bursts form in response to electrons accelerated by a shock produced when a coronal jet interacts with quiescent plasma at an interface.
