The escalating demands of quantum computing and communication systems necessitate the development of cryogenic cooling techniques capable of sustaining extremely low temperatures for an extended period. This study outlines a large millikelvin platform situated at Fermilab, designed to support the cooling needs of quantum computing and communication systems. The setup features a cryogenic refrigerator with a substantial cooling capacity, paired with a specially engineered vacuum chamber for temperature control and radiation shielding. The vacuum chamber's temperature can be maintained between 20 and 400 millikelvin in a stable manner. The successful achievement of this temperature requires approximately 1.4 liters per second of liquid helium consumption. The platform's innovative design incorporates an adjustable optical window for remote characterization and control, as well as a magnetic shield to facilitate the use of superconducting qubits in magnetic readout systems.

Previous research into misuses of cryptographic APIs has primarily relied on code reviews of open-source software, which offers limited insights into how these APIs are utilized within real-world applications. To address this, our study analyzed a vast collection of executable binaries, equivalent to approximately 180TB in size, to identify how developers misuse cryptographic functions in real-world scenarios. Our investigation involved a comprehensive analysis of 75 distinct misuses encountered in our dataset, which were categorized into 28 distinct root causes. Notably, our findings suggest that many misuses are often the result of insufficient library versions, outdated code, or inadequate validation of input parameters. Moreover, our study revealed that certain security vulnerabilities, such as plaintext disclosure and data tampering, can frequently arise from the same misuse. To enhance API security, our research provides recommendations for improving cryptographic function implementations, as well as suggestions for API hardening and softening.

The creation of accurate 3D models is crucial for various applications such as virtual planning, navigation, and environmental assessment. Current methods for generating 3D models are often influenced by personal biases and can be time-consuming and labor-intensive. This paper presents an innovative and efficient approach to 3D modeling, leveraging a large pool of independent contributors to produce a crowd-sourced model that minimizes personal biases. The proposed method utilizes a voting system to combine individual contributions from numerous contributors, resulting in a comprehensive and detailed 3D model. By crowdsourcing, this method benefits from the collective efforts of many contributors, reducing the overall workload and cost. The presented framework serves as a comprehensive guide, outlining procedures for data collection, pre-processing, and post-processing, as well as addressing potential issues and limitations associated with this approach.

We introduce a novel deep learning structure, the NuSPAN network, specifically
designed to solve the seismic reflectivity inversion problem through a nonuniform
sparse model approach. This method addresses the challenge of sparse seismic
data by learning a joint sparsity measure that incorporates nonuniform
penalties for different seismic samples. NuSPAN's architecture enables the
model to automatically adapt the sparsity measure at each layer, facilitating
the effective handling of varying noise levels across samples. Our approach
outperforms existing models by leveraging a nonuniform sparse objective in a
seismic inversion context.

This paper investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically on p-BMOA and its variant BMOA_s. We establish maximum principles for subharmonic functions to demonstrate that a semigroup of composition operators on BMOA_s is maximal, and that it has a equivalent representation on BMOA. We also derive sufficient and necessary conditions for the semigroup to be bounded on BMOA. Additionally, the paper examines the relationship between the given space and its analogue in terms of alpha-BMOA and alpha-BMOA_s. We establish that a composition operator on BMOA_s is bounded if and only if it is bounded on BMOA. We also investigate the maximal semigroup on BMOA_s corresponding to a Carathéodory prime, and provide a characterization of its closed subsemigroup.

A novel method is introduced to compute the coefficients of the effective Hamiltonian at the next-to-leading order, which describes the low-energy behavior of critical one-dimensional quantum systems. This method relies on the system's wave functions of the lowest modes and does not require knowledge of the system's wave functions at the leading order. Instead, it involves calculating the overlaps of these wave functions, which can often be achieved more easily. As a demonstration of this method's effectiveness, the research team applied it to the Haagerup model, a complex spin chain that defies solution via exact methods. Their results matched existing findings, including the model's central charge and critical exponents, which are essential characteristics of one-dimensional critical systems.

Automating part-of-speech (POS) annotation for language models has proven effective, yet models often fail when dealing with texts from earlier time periods. The chief reasons for this failure include the limited availability of training data, texts that are difficult to parse, and the evolution of language over time. The POS tagger developed using modern corpora often produces a substantial number of errors when applied to earlier texts. In response, researchers propose a novel approach that involves predicting a range of possible tags instead of a single outcome. The proposed method is based on the principle of minimizing the distance between the predicted and true tag sets. The method is tested using two historical corpora and is found to be more accurate than traditional single-value prediction methods.

This research explores a subset of non-invertible vector fields on a 2D surface, 
which correspond to a subset of symmetric differential operators on a 1D interval.
A specific metric is defined to measure the distance between such vector fields.
A phase space structure emerges, consisting of 2D surfaces linked by symplectic relationships.
This development leads to a new theory of symplectic geometry, distinct from the traditional smooth theory.
A specific example is provided, involving a hyperbolic circle, which serves as a prototype for understanding non-smooth phenomena.
This research uncovers novel features, such as the existence of smooth reference frames that are not symplectic.
It also reveals the existence of unique, non-smooth vector fields that are symplectic relative to specific reference frames.
These findings have implications for understanding the behavior of hyperbolic trajectories, as well as the properties of smooth symplectic transformations.

As cities' digital transformation progresses, more and not-so-technical citizens are expected to engage in providing services to city officials. To facilitate this, an easy-to-use system is needed to translate citizens' informal requirements into precise specifications. This paper presents a city requirements conversion assistant with a user-friendly interface, designed to help non-technical users specify formal requirements. The conversion process involves natural language understanding, requirement analysis, and design, and we present a case study demonstrating the effectiveness of this assistant.

A new approach called the hidden inverses protocol (HIP) has been developed to extend the coherence time of quantum devices by counteracting errors. This study investigates the efficacy of HIP on a particular quantum processor, examining its impact on different quantum operations. The authors also explore alternative methods to incorporate HIP into the processor's existing architecture. Their analysis, based on experimental data from a superconducting quantum device, suggests that HIP can notably improve the accuracy of specific quantum operations, while further research is needed to determine its effect on other operations.

In a general category $\mathbb E$, taking the direct image of a partial order under a surjective function often results in an equivalence relation. However, this property isn't inherent to every category. In a regular category $\mathbb C$, we're interested in understanding when the direct image of a partial order yields an equivalence relation. A partial solution to this problem involves considering the smallest equivalence relation containing the direct image, and we're investigating conditions under which this equivalence relation is generated by the direct image alone. A category $\mathbb C$ has the property $\mathbb C \mathbf{ERP}$ if taking the smallest equivalence relation of a partial order $P$ being equal to the direct image $f$ of $P$ happens consistently. In such cases, $\mathbb C$ also possesses unique properties including the category being well-powered and having a subobject closed $\lambda$-monoydian for some cardinal $\lambda$. A specific type of $\mathbb{C} \mathbf{ERP}$ category is defined as $\mathbb{C} \mathbf{ERP}_1$ in which taking the smallest equivalence relation of a partial order $P$ being equal to the direct image $f$ of $P$ happens when $f$ is a monomorphism. A key result shows that in a regular category $\mathbb C$, $\mathbb C$ is $\mathbb{C} \mathbf{ERP}_1$ if and only if

Using a joint multivariate spatial model for extreme events, we aim to forecast the likelihood of severe weather conditions in the Bass Strait, a crucial body of water connecting northeast Australia to the Torres Strait, known for generating extreme storms that pose significant threats to navigation and energy infrastructure. By combining data on extreme events and ocean pressure, we can accurately predict the occurrence of severe weather and assess the impact of extreme events on ship operations and wind energy production in the region. Our model accounts for dependencies between different types of extreme events, as well as their spatial correlation with weather patterns, including the influence of distant regions like the Lapetus Ocean. Through a simulation-based approach, we can evaluate the effectiveness of a new wind farm in reducing extreme events and assess the impact of severe weather on wind energy production and ship navigation.

Recently, Contrasting pre-trained image and text embeddings through projects like CLIP has gained significant interest due to its potential for fine-tuning without the need for extensive, meticulously labeled data - a major advantage. However, the current state of CLIP-based models falls short of expectations when it comes to tasks such as image captioning, primarily due to inaccuracies in text-image alignment. To address this limitation, we propose utilizing vision-derived textual cues to refine the text-image alignment, thereby enhancing the quality of visual-textual embeddings. Our approach, VT-CLIP, achieves this by introducing an unsupervised process to adapt initial text embeddings according to these cues. As a result, the text-image embeddings are improved, and performance in tasks like image captioning and zero-shot image classification is significantly boosted.

A particular method called the inverse problem theory offers a reliable approach for resolving noisy inverse problems in science, technology, and engineering. However, the availability of this approach is limited to specific types of problems, primarily those involving a large number of measurements. This study presents a new strategy, called the operator shifting technique, to extend the applicability of the inverse problem theory to a broader range of problems. By combining multiple measurements and employing an optimal approach, the operator shifting method effectively reduces the noise in matrices and their inverses. In addition to its versatility, the proposed method can be adapted to various types of noise and is suitable for large-scale problems involving matrices with a sparse or low-rank structure.

We calculate the slices of integral and Ext-based spectra in the quaternionic stable homotopy category, and we present a method for constructing a specific subcategory of spectra in this context. Our findings have an application in verifying the multiplicative form of the Miller--Sawin conjecture for the quaternionic homotopy category.

Given a Noetherian local ring with dimension d and depth d-1, we establish that its tight Hilbert function yields an r-rational Hilbert polynomial when the ring's r-rational Hilbert function has a non-reduced graded component, provided some additional conditions, including the ramification index, satisfy specific inequalities relative to r and d. This condition is met in established classes of local rings such as regular local rings and certain Gorenstein local rings with large depth. Consequently, we derive that the tight Hilbert function of such local rings is r-rational for all r > 1. Additionally, we demonstrate that our constructed tight Hilbert function agrees with the tight Hilbert function generated by the c-function for regular local rings and certain Gorenstein local rings meeting specific criteria, including those with large depth.

The application of machine learning in pathology and radiology has shown significant advancements, with the aim of making ML outputs interoperable with clinical data for patient benefit. However, current data formats hinder the sharing of ML results between systems, leading to a lack of standardization. To address this challenge, the open-source Highdicom library was created to develop a unified format for expressing ML outputs in radiology and pathology, with the potential to expand to other imaging modalities. Highdicom facilitates the conversion of ML outputs and other data into the DICOM and HL7 formats widely used in clinical settings. By integrating Highdicom into their workflows, researchers and developers can easily integrate their ML models with clinical imaging data, enabling more effective research and patient outcomes.

We have demonstrated that a specific Noether current can be constructed from the Einstein-Hilbert action's surface term, which leads to a virasoro algebra when the group of diffeomorphisms acts on it. This finding enables us to express the entropy of a black hole in terms of the news function, which is defined as the time-dependent component of the Weyl tensor.

In recent years, deep learning models have gained significant attention for their ability to analyze various genetic elements, including genes, exons, and enhancers, through the use of representation learning. However, the success of these models heavily relies on the quality and quantity of annotated data. This limitation becomes particularly pronounced when working with large, unannotated datasets. To address this challenge, our research introduces an innovative approach for extracting meaningful insights from large-scale, unsupervised DNA data. By combining a CNN model with a variable-length embedding and a distributed training process, our method is capable of learning accurate and biologically relevant representations for entire genomes. The efficacy of our model is demonstrated through successful classification tasks in the context of population genomics and genome-wide association studies.

The metal-insulator transitions of V$_2$O$_3$ films, encompassing various surface terminations, have been examined using in-situ transmission electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction, and low-energy electron diffraction. Our findings indicate that different surface terminations result in distinct growth behaviors and give rise to the same transition temperature of 170 K, but differ significantly in their electronic surface properties. A comparative analysis of the electronic structure of the terminations, conducted via scanning tunneling microscopy and photoemission spectroscopy, has provided valuable insight into the underlying mechanisms.

A new, systematic approach has been developed to canonize Lie-Poisson systems using Clebsch variables. This method provides a set of necessary and sufficient conditions to transform the reduced Hamiltonian and the Casimirs, as well as their differentials, into local coordinate functions. This method has been applied to a variety of differential equations, including fluid dynamics, to confirm previous results and reveal new findings about the structure of their symplectic manifolds. Furthermore, applications of this method to more complex systems, such as semidirect products, have been explored and used to canonize certain nonholonomic systems on a 3-dimensional sphere.

Our research presents an expanded list of gravitational microlensing planets identified by the KMTNet AnomalyFinder at prime fields for the years 2018-2020, increasing the known total to thirty-six, out of sixty-three planets discovered by the KMTNet, with half of the new findings being low-mass planet candidates. We analyzed the whole set of sixty-three planets, with a quarter being low-mass subsolar planets, revealing a significant trend of low mass planet primarity among KMTNet microlensing planet discoveries. We also observed a notable distribution of times of perihelion passage for the sample, with a concentration near 1 AU, and a significant number of planets having a perihelion distance between 0.7 and 1.0 AU, with a notable peak at 0.85 AU.

This study builds upon previously developed methods for modifying the solutions of conservative partial differential equations to achieve desired outcomes at a future time point. These methods involve input from an appropriate function and result in a minimal alteration to the initial data. It has been demonstrated that a broad class of input functions can lead to specific outcomes. Furthermore, it has been shown that the resulting function can be divided into components that can be easily calculated. The findings of this research are applied to the one-dimensional compressible Navier-Stokes equations, revealing that even with weak viscosity, it is possible to force the system into a specific state of equilibrium. The ability to achieve this outcome in a timely manner, without a significant change in initial conditions, and with minimal entropy over time is a significant consequence of our research.

This paper evaluates and compares the performance of several machine learning models, including KNN, Random Forest, and XGBoost, which were trained on data from non-performing loans in a bank's possession. The study examines the impact of pre-processing methods on model performance and assesses the effectiveness of different feature sets in predicting non-performing loans. Investigating how to curate and select features is a pressing issue in the machine learning community, and this research sheds light on its significance in financial contexts by analyzing the importance of each feature to the models.

The chromatic symmetric functions of Dyck paths are expressed in terms of the PEWES, a subset of the Shi or Schur semi-standard Young tableaux, which allows for a direct link between the PEWES and the q-counting principle known as q-rook theory as described by Stanley. This connection enables the computation of the chromatic symmetric functions' coefficients via the PEWES, thereby standardizing these coefficients. Furthermore, the coefficients' limits when the variable t tends towards infinity are found to be related to the central binomial coefficients. This is in line with similar results obtained by Han and Xu for Dyck lattice paths, and by Lecouvey and Lu for the k-Dyck paths. This study extends the findings of the aforementioned researchers by employing q-rook theory to derive explicit formulas for the coefficients, which are found to be in agreement with the previously established results.

Deep learning models, specifically convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have achieved remarkable success in image classification tasks by utilizing handcrafted image features. However, these features are inherently limited due to their reliance on traditional gradient-based methods. Our research introduces a novel approach, called orientation convolutional networks (OCNs), which leverages a unique transformation of image features to capture complex patterns within images. By applying a two-dimensional wavelet transform, we create multiple sub-bands and further apply a circular shift to each, enabling our OCNs to learn features at different orientations. Our OCNs are characterized by an empirical orthogonal transformation (EOT) filter, which can be jointly trained with other network components. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of OCNs in learning orientation-specific features, leading to improved performance in various image recognition tasks.

Using a novel relative trace formula, we investigate linear periods on $GL_{2n}$ that are modulated by a character. The key elements in this process involve establishing the relative fundamental lemma and the transfer of orbital integrals. Coupled with the Hironaka resolution of paradoxes, we successfully demonstrate the effectiveness of the new relative trace formula. Ultimately, we derive a comparison of the twisted linear periods associated with elliptic orbits via the spectral transfer of Hecke eigenvalues.

Within the context of the Standard Model, we examine the connection between the pole mass and the running mass of the top quark, taking into account higher-order corrections from QCD and electroweak interactions, as well as the impact of mass effects in the renormalization group equation on the top quark's pole mass. Our analysis considers the standard choice of parameterization and two alternative methods that employ the Villani, ABJ, and ABJ(R) parameters. By integrating the impact of mass effects into the renormalization of the top quark's Yukawa parameter, we ensure that the ratio $\hat m_t/\bar m_t$ meets the decoupling limit criteria. Our findings, accurate to fifth order in the strong coupling constant, reveal that the ABJ(R) parameterization yields results that are essentially independent of the light quark masses, with differences between this and the standard parameterization amounting to less than a 10 MeV contribution to the top quark's pole mass.

Consider a graph $G$ and a subset $R$ of its vertices $V(G)$. A specific edge coloring of $G$ with colors from 1 to $t$ is called an $R$-sequential $t$-coloring when each vertex $v$ in $R$ uses distinct colors from its previous $t-1$ closest neighbors in $R$. Here, we investigate the possibility and study the least number of colors required for an $R$-sequential $t$-coloring, denoted as $\chi_{R}^{\ast}(G)$, and provide some upper bounds based on the degree of $G$ and the number of vertices in $R$. Additionally, we explore some related problems and provide some specific results for particular types of graphs.

We establish a precise relationship between L^p to L^q contraction inequalities in weighted Bergman spaces over the unit disk, incorporating typical weight factors and α > 1. This outcome addresses an unresolved issue in reference \cite{JANSON}, with the added consideration of cases where q is greater than or equal to 2, while providing related estimates for the more complex situation of multiple contractions.

The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has led to widespread infections and severe hospitalizations, straining healthcare systems worldwide. As the number of infections continues to rise, there is an urgent need for a reliable and efficient diagnostic method to contain the outbreak. Computed tomography (CT) scans have been widely adopted as a primary diagnostic tool for COVID-19, detecting associated interstitial patterns. However, conventional CT scans expose patients to high levels of radiation, which can be hazardous, especially for vulnerable groups. Low-dose and time-differential CT scans have been proposed as safer alternatives, aiming to enhance the accuracy of COVID-19 diagnosis. Researchers have developed a groundbreaking two-stage capsule network model that leverages these safer scanning methods to produce human-level performance. By combining the capabilities of a spatial capsule network and a temporal capsule network, this model can accurately detect COVID-19 from low-dose and time-differential CT scans, achieving an impressive performance equivalent to that of experienced radiologists.

In the rapidly expanding space industry, the issue of crowded low-Earth orbit (LEO) is becoming a significant concern that must be addressed. This region, serving as a primary launch site and home to numerous small satellites, is experiencing a surge in satellite deployments. As a result, a shortage of available orbital space has emerged, posing a significant challenge to mission planners. To mitigate these challenges, it is essential to understand the dynamics of space occupancy in LEO. This study aims to develop a mathematical framework for modeling space occupancy in LEO, where we define space occupancy as the probability that a randomly selected point within a given sphere or shell is occupied by a satellite. To calculate this probability, we employ a Poisson point process representing satellite distributions and characterize the associated random variables. Furthermore, we derive analytical approximations for space occupancy in both radial and tangential directions, demonstrating good correspondence with simulation-based estimates. By integrating these models into a mission planner's workflow, we can help reduce the likelihood of collisions and mitigate their adverse effects, such as radio interference.

A crucial step in the simulation process is generating a discrete mesh that accurately represents the physical object in question. For complex shapes defined by parametric functions and topological structures, we have developed an efficient method to produce high-quality quadrilateral meshes. Our approach leverages combinatorial optimization techniques to create mesh cells and their respective topology, taking full advantage of the object's inherent structure. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of this method in producing high-quality meshes with minimal cells.

This research presents a novel theoretical approach to calculate the sample correlation coefficient's moments, taking into account data point permutations. Building on the associated distribution's moment-cumulant diagrams, we derived closed-form analytical expressions for the zero, first, second, third, fourth, and sixth moments, along with associated central skewness and kurtosis. We found that, under certain conditions, the sample correlation coefficient approximates normality due to its asymptotic behavior. Additionally, we used these moment results to estimate the associated distribution's cumulants. While our findings are applicable to any data set, we conducted a thorough analysis focusing on Gaussian-distributed variables, given the sample correlation coefficient's well-behavior in this context.

We detail the reasoning behind implementing a quantum S-matrix framework for tackling classical gravitational scattering between two bodies. Furthermore, a method is briefly outlined for computing black hole metrics across multiple spatial dimensions.

We examine the two-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations with weak or strong forcing terms within specific functional spaces. A controlled system is obtained by incorporating a finite dimensional feedback control in the velocity equation. We demonstrate that this system exhibits uniform stabilization, using a novel approach that differs from existing methods. This entails establishing a specific estimate for the velocity error using a control with limited support. To achieve this, we apply a combination of mathematical techniques, including a specific decomposition of the velocity error, a modified version of a key inequality in P. Constantin and C. Foias' book, and a specific regularity result for solutions to a related linear equation.

Language learning dictionaries are highly beneficial tools that facilitate vocabulary development and grammatical proficiency. However, conventional dictionaries often fall short by not providing sufficient context for understanding word meanings. To address this, we have developed LitMind, a cutting-edge online dictionary that offers a more comprehensive and context-aware learning experience. Powered by a neural network language model, LitMind dynamically curates definitions, examples, and context-specific word usage from a massive language dataset. Furthermore, it allows users to search words by part of speech, enabling learners to discover alternative word choices. With its user-friendly interface and robust mobile optimization, LitMind is accessible on any device and can be easily installed from a public GitHub repository for further community-driven development.

The growing interest in transparent AI has led to an increase in research on explainable recommendation systems. Among these, post-hoc methods have gained traction due to their ease of implementation and adaptability. A recently developed technique combines local surrogate modeling with sensitivity analysis to provide feature-weighted importances. This study introduces two enhancements to this method, addressing limitations in feature stabilization and prediction consistency. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our modified approach in terms of prediction stability and overall accuracy.

Quantum devices based on superconducting properties are highly sensitive to variations in their internal environment. Researchers are investigating unique quantum wells, such as InAs/GaAs, to take advantage of their potential for superconductivity. These quantum wells have a distinctive structure, with the indium atoms closer to the surface, which influences their behavior. To gain a deeper understanding, researchers studied the properties of the surface of these quantum wells by examining the photoemission spectra of the relevant area. This led to the discovery that the surface of these quantum wells becomes pinned at specific points within the bandgap, which has significant implications for the movement of charge carriers across the surface. This pinning has important consequences for the movement of charge carriers across the surface, particularly for the movement of charge carriers across the surface.

The success of machine learning algorithms has sparked interest in developing algorithms that can effectively navigate diverse and complex environments. Research has shown that local query algorithms, which ask for information about specific examples, can improve performance on challenging tasks. However, the potential benefits of local queries for learning fair and robust models remain unclear. In this study, we investigate the conditions under which local queries can help achieve these goals by analyzing a simple yet versatile class of local queries. Our findings reveal that local queries are particularly beneficial when the data contains significant biases and obstacles to learning, such as adversarial noise and complex relationships. In contrast, local queries offer minimal advantages when the data is relatively straightforward and easy to analyze.

Our previous research significantly sped up Sinkhorn iteration by applying a specific kernel matrix. This time, we've developed an even more efficient version of the algorithm, utilizing a kernel matrix with triangular structure that allows for quick computation via solving a tri-diagonal eigenvalue problem. This advancement enables the solution of the optimal transport problem in an optimal number of iterations, with computational complexity reduced to linear time and dependent on the number of iterations needed for convergence. This novel matrix has a distinct band structure that facilitates efficient inverting, making the Sinkhorn algorithm even faster.

The AU Mic system offers an optimal setting for studying young stars and their habitable zones due to its closeness and high brightness. Observations conducted over 10 years with the GALEX and IUE provide valuable insights into the star's behavior in the UV spectrum, complemented by recent FUV observations in quiescence and during flares using the GOLDFISH instrument on the Telescopio Secondo Pier. Analysis of these observations reveals that AU Mic's UV radiation exhibits significant variability, with its energy output potentially exceeding that of Jupiter's moon Io. These findings suggest that the planet AU Mic b, with its estimated mass similar to Io's, may experience surface heating similar to that observed on Io, with potential implications for its habitability.

We've discovered that when charged particles move quickly through a medium that resists changes, it loses kinetic energy at a faster rate due to the medium's resistance than it would in a vacuum. We've developed an exact mathematical formula to calculate this energy loss for particles moving in any direction as a result of the medium's resistance for both non-relativistic and ultra-relativistic particles. We've also identified the conditions under which the energy loss is symmetrical and uniform. We've also derived a simplified mathematical formula for a specific type of medium and found that the simplified formula is close enough to the exact one for most practical purposes. We've also calculated the time it takes for a particle to lose its kinetic energy for both types of particles and found that the simplified formula works well under most conditions.

In the context of an unevenly distributed classification problem, most popular loss functions for the t-statistic and nearest neighbor methods have biased performance. We propose an innovative nearest neighbor classification approach that achieves balanced performance and works with any type of loss function. The new method's performance with a range of loss functions is evaluated, and we find that using the minimum Mahalanobis distance delivers consistent results and asymptotically balanced results. A simulation study demonstrates the proposed method's effectiveness in achieving majority class parity.

Our analysis of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey's data and observations by the SkyMapper telescope has yielded 15 newly discovered high-redshift quasars at redshifts exceeding 5.5, with a significant majority residing in the redshift range of 6 to 7.5. These newly discovered objects, coupled with an updated sample of 34 quasars observed by SkyMapper, have expanded our knowledge of the luminosity function's bright end. Our research indicates that the luminosity function's shape remains relatively consistent across this range, with a notable deviation from a single power-law model. The study's findings are supported by a significant correlation between the quasars' luminosities and their characteristic spectral features, with a notable absence of objects at the luminosity peak when compared to lower-redshift samples. The study's results are consistent with a scenario in which the quasars' fuel supply is rapidly depleted, with implications for our understanding of the quasars' evolution and the formation of massive galaxies. The study's findings are further supported by a correlation between the quasars' luminosity and their characteristic emission lines, with a notable absence of objects at the luminosity peak when compared to lower-redshift samples. The study's results are consistent with a scenario in which the quasars' fuel supply is rapidly depleted, with implications for our understanding of the quasars' evolution and the formation of massive galaxies.

The connection between a quantum dot and an superconducting island on an island within a hybrid system is examined through the movement of charges, ultimately revealing the emergence of multiple distinct tunneling processes. Specifically, this hybrid system's behavior can be observed transitioning from a conventional tunneling regime to a hybrid process known as Josephson tunneling as the hybridization strength increases. Furthermore, this hybrid system's behavior can also be studied by analyzing the movement of charges under different applied bias conditions, thus confirming that hybrid tunneling exists. The conventional and hybrid tunneling processes are found to have distinct effects on the movement of charges across the hybrid system, with conventional tunneling primarily affecting charge movement at higher temperatures, while hybrid tunneling dominates at lower hybridization strengths and lower temperatures.

Our research offers new requirements for systems of conservation laws that enable the analysis of solutions with discontinuities using an entropy approach, provided those solutions meet certain conditions initially and the system complies with a specific technical criterion. Building upon our earlier work with Chandrashekar S. and Kholkin A., we relax an existing restriction related to the system's structure and its initial conditions, enabling the analysis to be extended to a broader class of systems, including ones that exhibit a unique characteristic, known as the Helmholtz condition. To achieve this, we establish a relationship between the properties of the system's energy and entropy, allowing for the analysis of solutions with certain characteristics, even when the usual Lax-Friedrichs condition is not met. Our findings are illustrated by the application to a model of compressible stars, which cannot be analyzed using the Lax-Friedrichs condition due to its degenerate nature.

We propose the DiffDreamer, a novel view generator that produces highly accurate and consistent views given a camera's previous position and a new target location. The model achieves this by learning a latent space that corresponds to real images, allowing it to generate views with high fidelity and detail. The method's training involves teaching the model to recover the original image's latent representation from a distorted version, created by applying a camera transformation to the image. This enables the model to estimate latent representations for any camera configuration, including those that were not encountered during training. We demonstrate the model's capabilities using indoor images and compare its performance favorably against existing methods.

A novel mathematical approach has been developed that translates complex interconnected system observations into functional descriptions of their underlying dynamics. This framework enables prediction, optimization, and control by transforming raw data into a universal model. To demonstrate its effectiveness, the approach was successfully applied to an epidemic model (EIS), which models the spread of diseases. This model consists of various interconnected networks representing different types of close relationships, such as within households or neighborhoods. By using the approach on observed epidemic model data, accurate predictions of outbreaks and optimal resource allocations for limited interventions can be made, showing universal applicability to any network process. This method was verified using synthetic data and also tested using real COVID-19 contact network data from Los Angeles County, showing potential benefits for disease control.

The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This understanding has led to a theoretical model that uses the axisymmetric Stokes equations to examine the effect of liquid-solid slip on a film undergoing the Rayleigh-Plateau instability. The analysis reveals that significant decreases in the boundary layer thickness lead to increased instability, which is similar to that observed in a solid melt. However, in cases where the boundary layer thickness is greater than the wavelength of the instability, the instability is intensified, with a shift in the Laplace pressure in the air compared to that in the melt. This results in a larger first-order correction to the energy change, which could lead to a more rapid decrease in the film's radius.

We investigate the temporal Lipschitz stability for solutions of the Hunter-Saxton equation, focusing on $\alpha$-dissipative solutions with $\alpha$ a constant in the interval $[0,1]$. We introduce and study the properties of a metric both in a general context and with specific considerations for Lipschitz stability, including applications to solutions with fixed points. We demonstrate the Lipschitz stability for the full range of $\alpha$ in the case of $C^0$-analogues and provide a metric that works for any value of $\alpha$. We further show the Lipschitz stability for $W^{1,\infty}$-analogues of solutions with fixed points when $\alpha$ can take any value up to 1.

Evaluating scoliosis using ultrasound-based side-bending assessment can be an onerous task, especially when relying on manual ultrasound scans. To alleviate this, a study compared robotic scanning with manual scanning for reliability. Scoliosis assessments via ultrasound have been challenging due to the device's limitations, making side-bending evaluations a labor-intensive task. To address this issue, robotic scanning was tested alongside manual scanning in assessing scoliosis, with both methods yielding comparable results. Robotic scanning not only facilitates scoliosis assessments but also reduces the strain associated with using ultrasound technology, making it a more efficient and reliable tool for side-bending evaluations.

This study introduces a novel method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations, this method leverages a median-based objective to handle skewed distributions and employs a non-parametric technique for modelling uncertain future states. We showcase the effectiveness of this method using the CASA corpus, highlighting its ability to handle rare events and low-probability phone sequences.

In the realm of Social Media Studies, hate speech has been a long-standing concern, leading to severe consequences for individuals and societal cohesion. Despite its significance, data scarcity has hindered research in this area. To bridge this gap, we have developed a novel machine learning model for identifying hate speech, utilizing a large dataset of 35K comments. Our approach differs from existing models by leveraging a unique feature engineering method that enhances performance. Additionally, we have created an efficient model to optimize the model's parameters. Our model's exceptional results, comprising macro-averaged F1 scores of 72.1% for classification and 68.6% for toxicity detection, establish a new benchmark in their respective categories.

Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) architectures, widely used in computer vision and deep learning, can be inefficient due to redundant computations in their initial stages. These redundancies are particularly pronounced in the first layers of the model, leading to significant waste of resources. To address this issue, implementing data parallelism in the initial stages would reduce memory requirements, but this is impractical due to the large number of redundant computations. A more viable approach is to eliminate the parallelism at the data level and instead optimize the model architecture to minimize resource waste. For instance, using a single-head instead of multiple heads in the first layer would reduce the memory footprint. However, this would result in a substantial decrease in processing power, requiring a faster CPU to accommodate the increased workload without increasing memory usage. A novel approach has been proposed to strike a balance between processing power and memory usage in MIMO architectures. The proposed method, called shared head, involves splitting the first layer into separate sub-tensors and assigning each one to a unique head, thereby reducing parallelism and memory requirements while maintaining a stable workload. This architecture has been implemented and tested on multiple models, demonstrating an improved efficiency. The results show that the proposed model achieves a better performance on ImageNet-1K using the same hardware as the original MIMO architecture, and also outperforms a CPU with a higher core capacity.

This study offers a comprehensive review of the most notable datasets used for research in historical document image analysis. It presents a thorough examination of several influential datasets through an assessment of their completeness, accuracy, and presentation quality. Additionally, the paper outlines existing tools for ground truth creation and suggests potential areas for advancement in this area. Ultimately, the paper provides an analysis of the strengths and limitations of the datasets reviewed.

This study proposes a straightforward and effective control strategy for an industrial robot joint, utilizing information from secondary position sensors. The approach is based on a linearization technique, which is derived from the fundamental equations of the robot model. The development of a linear control strategy using the proposed linearization, has shown to be as efficient as other advanced nonlinear control methods, yet is simpler to implement and requires less computational power. Moreover, this strategy can be easily adapted to systems with complex dynamics, even when model parameters are uncertain. The research demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed strategy through both simulation and real-world testing, highlighting its benefits in practical applications.

A novel statistical method, known as Multiple State Analysis, is designed to
handle complex patterns of repeated events and is particularly useful in
medical research where individuals may experience multiple health issues.
This approach is essential for understanding how different factors contribute to
various health problems, especially when dealing with multiple types of events.
To demonstrate its effectiveness, a Multiple State Analysis was used to
investigate the factors leading to multiple myocardial infarctions, and the
results showed that certain factors, such as hypertension and heart disease, can
increase the risk of subsequent infarctions.
This innovative method offers a comprehensive way to analyze life-long health
patterns and identify the underlying causes of repeated health issues.
A software package, named MSa, has been developed to facilitate the use of
Multiple State Analysis and is available for free at the website:
http://www.msanalysis.org.

A novel quadrature technique has been developed for efficient integration within molecular simulations. This method effectively handles molecular interactions by using a specially designed scheme where quadrature points adapt to the environment. This adaptation enables better representation of molecular forces. This approach ensures mass conservation and maintains stability in the simulation, accurately modeling molecular dynamics. Several key factors, including the type of basis sets, the location of quadrature points, and the maximum time step, have been rigorously examined to ensure accuracy and numerical stability. This method demonstrates promising results, particularly when using a multi-center scheme, which significantly outperforms traditional finite difference methods, especially at large time step sizes.

A vector space dimension parameter known as the metric dimension, or MD, quantifies a set of points using a minimum number of special probes to fully identify any point location using a specific set of locations. The problem of determining the minimum dimension required to identify all point locations is NP-complete, and research has explored its complexity in relation to other structural parameters. This study investigates the complexity of determining the minimum dimension required to identify all point locations, and finds it to be W[1]-hard when parameterized by several structural parameters, including feedback vertex number, hole number, and cluster number. The study also establishes a polynomial-time algorithm parameterized by the size of the feedback vertex set and displays the applicability of this parameter in designing more efficient algorithms.

Power spaces, introduced by Brezis and Petrosyan, consist of pairs of functions along with a relation that satisfies specific inequality conditions. These spaces have the potential to be used as a mathematical model for Nash equilibria in game theory. Our work extends the power structure concept to directed spaces, allowing for the definition of upper and lower Dirichlet orders. This leads to the discovery of a power structure on directed spaces, characterized by the upper Dirichlet order. Additionally, we investigate the properties of power spaces, finding that the closure of the graph of a function, where the function is upper semi-continuous, results in a complete directed upper power continuity space. Our study also defines Green's relations on the set of all continuous power mappings and shows that the set forms a semigroup under composition.

Past Earth climates, known as "hothouse" climates, were much warmer than they are today, with significant differences in how sunlight and precipitation were distributed around the globe.  To better understand these climates, we used computer models to simulate them, and found that they were characterized by unusual patterns of precipitation that varied greatly from those of the present day.  This led to the creation of a new metric to quantify the variability in precipitation patterns.  Our analysis of the simulations showed that the most extreme precipitation occurred at high latitudes, with massive downpours that lasted for only a short time.  This was followed by a dry period.  Our results suggest that the early history of Earth may have been characterized by frequent and intense precipitation events that varied greatly from one area to another.

We have established Twistor actions for self-dual Yang-Mills theory and its spin extensions in five and eleven dimensions. These constructions align with existing work on Yang-Mills theory, yet offer a novel approach using Twistor actions specifically suited for high-energy scattering calculations. We have also explored the free high-spin theory as an extension of this work.

Recent advancements in deep learning have shown that large medical image datasets can lead to high-performing diagnostic capabilities, but the accuracy of these models heavily depends on the quality of the labels. In reality, labels are often flawed due to various inaccuracies and inconsistencies, which in turn affect the performance of the models. In this paper, we present a novel approach called Bayesian Statistics Guided Label Refurbishment (BSGLR) that aims to improve the accuracy of labels by leveraging the statistical analysis of the models. The proposed method involves two key steps: first, it identifies potentially unreliable labels by examining the models' probability distributions, and second, it refurbishes the labels by applying a statistical reassignment technique. The efficacy of the BSGLR method was tested using the NIH Chest X-Ray-14 dataset, which showed that it effectively mitigates label noise and enhances the performance of the models.

Consider a unit cube, $Q_n$, in $n$-dimensional space and a function space, $C(Q_n)$, consisting of continuous functions from $Q_n$ to $\mathbb{R}$. Let $\Pi_h$ be an interpolation projector that maps functions from $C(Q_n)$ to a space of piecewise polynomials, mapping functions with continuous values on $Q_n$ to values at a finite set of points. The maximum distance between a function and its interpolation can be estimated as follows: for any function $f$ in $C(Q_n)$, the distance between $f$ and $\Pi_h(f)$ does not exceed $2\sqrt{n}$ times the distance between the function values at the points where the interpolation is performed. This estimate is sharp.

A correlated random walk (CRW) is derived from the Grover matrix, the evolution matrix of the Grover walk on a graph G, and an arbitrary initial state. The associated transition probability matrix (TPM) has elements that are the probabilities of reaching a specific vertex given a particular initial state. The purpose of this research is to explore properties of the TPM, specifically in terms of eigenvalues and eigenfunctions, relating to the real eigenfunctions associated with the eigenvalues less than one in magnitude. The work builds on existing research by J. Grannell et al. and J. Wallis, focusing on real eigenfunctions related to the Frobenius-Khashin eigenfunctions associated with eigenvalues less than one in magnitude. The research uses a novel approach by examining real eigenfunctions related to the largest Frobenius-Khashin eigenvalues, and a new real eigenfunction is established for regular graphs when the initial state is arbitrary. The research also generalizes previous findings by Grannell et al. and Wallis in the context of real eigenfunctions related to the largest Frobenius-Khashin eigenvalues, and a new real eigenfunction is established for regular graphs when the initial state is arbitrary. The research further demonstrates that the eigenvalues of the TPM at zero, denoted as $\tau_0$, are linked to the real eigenfunctions associated with the largest Frobenius-Khashin eigenvalues, and a new formula is established for $\tau_0$ in

In a total functions logic such as HOL, certain non-terminating functions cannot be directly defined. To overcome this limitation, a clock function is introduced to terminate recursive definitions, but this requires extra effort to choose an appropriate clock that doesn't interfere with the logic. To simplify clock function management, a theorem is developed in HOL that allows for the automatic conversion of certain total functions into a more clock-friendly format, enabling more effortless use of recursive definitions in HOL.

Coherent structure-based models have been widely used to predict wall turbulence in engineering and scientific research, offering a unique perspective among the various modeling approaches. Despite their success in capturing the overall trend of wall pressure and velocity, these models have fallen short of accurately predicting instantaneous wall conditions. To bridge this gap, researchers have employed machine learning algorithms to analyze and interpret the large datasets generated by simulations. By applying a deep learning technique to identify and classify the intricate patterns in instantaneous wall data, researchers have been able to enhance coherent structure-based models and achieve more precise predictions. The results demonstrate that this combination of models can accurately predict instantaneous wall conditions, even outperforming simulation results in some cases.

Researchers have explored soliton solutions in Skyrme models with a Born-Infeld profile, discovering that the profile's constraints are eased due to its gauge invariance properties. The resulting model allows for the coexistence of topological and symmetry-protected solitons. In this model, we find solutions that balance Skyrme and Born-Infeld characteristics and possess self-dual properties. The model also exhibits a new type of topological charge, distinct from the Skyrme model's non-abelian sector, which instead mirrors the properties of the abelian sector.

In three-dimensional systems with a twist, such as those experiencing a magnetic field, Weyl semimetals have been found to possess both time-reversal and spatial periodicity breakdowns. We investigated the impact of this combined breakdown by studying the electronic properties of a three-dimensional tight-binding model under strong magnetic fields. Our results show that as the magnetic field's strength increases, new phases emerge in the phase diagram, including phases characterized by uniform and half uniform charge density. These new phases are distinguished by the simultaneous occurrence of a van Hove singularity and a half uniform charge density, features that cannot be found in three-dimensional systems under a uniform magnetic field. We also demonstrated that the time-reversal-broken nature of these states can be verified by examining the Berry curvature distribution in the momentum space.

This research proposes a unique optical nanoantenna that combines both dielectric and plasmonic components, capable of efficiently emitting unidirectional light. The design leverages a HOMO/LUMO gap energy source and incorporates a narrow aperture for directed light emission. The dielectric component minimizes energy loss typically associated with plasmonic nanoantennas, while the plasmonic part enhances the antenna's effective light emission. The study demonstrates that this hybrid antenna can achieve high radiative efficiency and increased brightness. The findings suggest that dielectric-plasmonic nanoantennas could be an essential component in solid-state sources, directional emitters, and quantum communication systems.

Electrostatic screening in granular media, such as sandpits, displays unique properties due to the non-conductive and irregularly-shaped grains, resulting in a more complex phenomenon than expected in conductive fluids. The phenomenon can be understood by considering the grains as non-interacting point charges. At a large scale, this system behaves according to a theoretical model derived from Poisson's equation, where the screening length is inversely proportional to the square root of the average electrostatic potential energy. Our research supports this model through experiments and numerical simulations, showing that the screening length is related to the average electrostatic potential energy in granular matter.

Utilizing first-principles calculations, our research involves analyzing silicene in relation to hexagonal boron nitride substrates. Hexagonal boron nitride, being a semiconductor, doesn't affect silicene's metallic nature. Additionally, our study includes the results of decorating hexagonal boron nitride with manganese atoms, resulting in three-layer systems consisting of manganese-decorated silicene layers and one monolayer of hexagonal boron nitride. Notably, our findings indicate that these systems are stable and have transferable properties, such as their band structures and charge density distributions.

A long-standing enigma surrounds Sgr A East, a radiating supernova remnant situated near the center of the Milky Way, with estimates of its age ranging from 1,000 to 150,000 years. Researchers have proposed that the explosion of a massive star or core collapse triggered the event, but the actual age and origin remain unclear. A recent study suggests that the supernova that created Sgr A East occurred in the Sagittarius Arm of the galaxy, near Kojima's star, a luminous star located approximately 2 parsecs from the remnant's center. Analysis of the star's brightness and motion suggests that it may be part of Sgr A East's shell, and its location could indicate the site of a supernova that occurred around 1,000 to 10,000 years ago.

The study examines various oversampling methods to classify multi-class topics, particularly focusing on the performance of SMOTE, a method that creates new samples by combining existing ones, and its two variants along with random oversampling approach in text classification. The findings reveal that SMOTE has a significant impact on the accuracy of naive Bayes and k-nearest neighbors classifiers, leading to improved performance compared to random oversampling. Notably, the best results were achieved by combining SMOTE with k-nearest neighbors classifier, which experienced a notable increase in accuracy up to 8% after data resampling.

This study examines the connections between local news coverage, the COVID-19 pandemic's impact, and broadcasting patterns in the United States. It analyzes data from news broadcasts and the COVID's effects on 96 U.S. cities between August 2019 and July 2020. The research found a positive correlation between the news coverage and the number of cases and deaths in the cities. However, it also discovered a negative relationship between the news coverage and the speed at which the virus spread, suggesting that increased attention may have initially delayed the outbreak but ultimately contributed to its eventual decline. The study also revealed differences in the response of local and national news outlets to the pandemic, with local news covering the virus more extensively but national news covering its social and economic consequences more thoroughly. Furthermore, it found that the news coverage varied significantly depending on the city's demographics, with news in cities facing more severe outbreaks focusing more on the health aspects and those with fewer cases focusing on the social and economic aspects.

Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses inherent conservation capabilities, making it ideal for complex simulations. However, accurate maintenance of angular momentum is often compromised in pursuit of increased efficiency, resulting in inaccuracies and energy errors. This paper proposes a modification to the fast multipole method for SPH that adheres to angular momentum conservation. By leveraging the conservation properties of this method, our approach ensures that angular momentum is precisely maintained at a cost equivalent to the original implementation. The resulting innovation boasts improved precision and reduced energy errors, particularly beneficial for detailed, long-term simulations.

Research has revealed an intriguing phenomenon where the polarization of the initial proton is transferred to the final proton in the $e\vec{p} \to e\vec{p}$ process within the quasielastic region. This transfer occurs selectively, favoring either the perpendicular or parallel polarization state of the proton. The underlying cause of this selectivity lies in the distinct characteristics of the single nucleon knock-out mechanism and the coherent virtual photon-nucleon interaction. The latter effectively acts as a unitary transformation, thereby preserving the overall polarization of the proton. The calculated cross-section ratios for the $^{12}$C to $^{12}$C inclusive $e\vec{p} \to e\vec{p}$ process show striking agreement with the data obtained through polarization analysis of the proton.

To achieve the best results, it's beneficial to combine multiple approaches. Specifically, when it comes to learning, utilizing multiple experts along with a head that binds them together can lead to improved performance. However, when it comes to complex tasks, it can be impractical to have multiple experts. To solve this issue, we propose a method that allows existing models to be modified so they can serve as experts, and then uses a head to learn from these models. To make the most of this method, we've developed a technique that increases the effectiveness of the training process by generating artificial data. This technique works by applying random transformations to the original dataset. To ensure that these artificially created examples don't mislead the head, we've also developed a way to measure how certain they are. This allows us to train the head to rely on the most confident predictions. Our proposed method has been tested on multiple tasks, and the results show that it's an effective way to leverage existing models and speed up the training process.

A comprehensive study of the creation of two Higgs bosons ($hh$) paired with a vector boson ($W$ or $Z$) using a massive dataset of 139 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collisions at a 13 TeV energy has been conducted. Utilizing a 2015-2018 dataset collected with the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider, researchers investigated final states featuring two, three, or four massive bosons. To identify the target signal, researchers employed advanced techniques to distinguish the $hh$ resonance from the background using a combination of kinematic variables. To validate the analysis, simulated data were used to mimic the conditions of the experiment. To summarize, researchers observed an excess of events corresponding to approximately 0.3 standard deviations above the predicted background levels in the search for the $q\bar{q}(\ell\nu) + hh$ channel. To summarize, researchers observed an excess of events corresponding to approximately 0.3 standard deviations above the predicted background levels in the search for the $q\bar{q}(\ell\nu) + hh$ channel. To explore the expected outcomes, researchers derived upper bounds on the predicted cross-sections for the creation of $Vhh$ pairs at various Higgs boson pair production levels.
